utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar, please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours; good afternoon everyone in and around the courtroom. This is case number IT-04-74-T, the Prosecutor versus Prlic et al. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Registrar. Today is Wednesday, 7th of May. Good afternoon to the Prosecution, to the Defence counsel, to the accused, and to all the people assisting us in our work. For your information, Mr. Karnavas, you used one hour, 19 minutes, so you can add up, and you'll see how much time you have left. Let's have the witness in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, sir. We are going to resume the examination-in-chief. You have the floor. You may proceed, Mr. Karnavas.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Good afternoon, Your Honours and everyone in and around the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And good afternoon, Mr. Zuzul. Welcome back. I trust you had a good evening. Now, yesterday when we left off, I'd asked you a question about the concept of confederation, and it was at that point when you were just about to finish your answer when we had to stop for the day. We will discuss in great detail this concept, but with respect to the concept of confederation, did President Tudjman and President Izetbegovic ever sign any agreements concerning that?

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR ZUZUL [Resumed]
utterances.text: President Tudjman, President Izetbegovic signed a mutual agreement on the confederation. I believe that was on the 14th of September, 1993. The decision was taken that the agreement would be kept secret in a way. It was never made public. Each of the presidents kept a copy, and there was another one kept at the mission of the Republic of Croatia at Geneva.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR ZUZUL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Needless to say, I am well aware of the existence of that agreement because I was involved in preparing it, and I actually physically drafted it myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, we'll discuss that later on towards the end of your testimony here today, but just to round off this topic, are you aware whether President Izetbegovic ever signed any other agreements with others that would impact or had anything to do with the agreement that you've just indicated to us?

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR ZUZUL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. A mere two days later, President Izetbegovic signed an agreement with Mr. Karadzic. It was a similar agreement, but it wasn't about a confederation. It was about creating republics within the union. The most noteworthy feature of that agreement was this: First of all, Izetbegovic took this step without ever mentioning it to the Croatian side, or at least not to President Tudjman. Secondly, the substance of the agreement itself. What is noteworthy is the fact that President Izetbegovic subscribed to the possibility that after two years the Serbs would be allowed to leave the union. The possibility, in other words, for Bosnia and Herzegovina to break up.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. And we're going to get to that, as well, but I just want to make sure I'm crystal clear here and that the Judges understand this. What you're telling us is this: That the second agreement between Izetbegovic, two days later that is, and the Serbs called for the possibility of an eventual carving up of Bosnia-Herzegovina two years after that agreement; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR ZUZUL [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, finally before we get into the documents, and when we do so we'll be going through them rather quickly, but finally were you ever present when Izetbegovic offered any other part of Bosnia and Herzegovina to anyone else, because it would seem to me that based on this agreement he's offering the Serbs a piece of Bosnia and Herzegovina. Did he ever offer any other part of Bosnia and Herzegovina to anyone else and, if so, to whom?

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR ZUZUL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was present in Geneva, I think, in the spring of 1993, just before this when President Izetbegovic made a direct proposal to President Tudjman for Western Herzegovina to be annexed by Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR ZUZUL [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was during a recess in the Geneva negotiations. I was with President Tudjman, and we approached President Izetbegovic. This was something that often happened during recesses in negotiations. At a meeting that had just taken place, there had been very unpleasant conversation where the Bosniak side with President Izetbegovic and the Serbs clashed. I think it was purely human reasons that motivated or pushed Tudjman to approach Izetbegovic during that recess. I can't remember specifically who was with President Izetbegovic. I do believe that Mr. Miles Raguz was also with him at the time. They talked and President Izetbegovic made a proposal in no uncertain terms about what I just said, for Western Herzegovina to secede from Bosnia and Herzegovina and join Croatia. He wasn't specific about the precise extent of the territory on offer. Nonetheless, President Tudjman refused to talk about this. Later on after we'd left, at lunch the president continued to talk about this. My impression at the time was he had been somewhat taken aback by this. He nevertheless believed that regardless of Izetbegovic's motives for that proposal this could never be an appropriate solution for dealing with the crisis in Bosnia and Herzegovina, nor indeed could it be a solution for the status of the Croats in Bosnia and Herzegovina. Some time later, perhaps a year or more later, I brought this anecdote up with Minister Granic who at the time was Croatia's Foreign Minister. He then shared with me that he, too, once had attended a meeting at which President Izetbegovic tabled a similar proposal. This other proposal that Minister Granic was now telling me about was even more specific in purely territorial terms. There was talk of specific municipalities that would make up this territory. Nonetheless, at least based on what Granic told me at the time, Tudjman yet again refused to discuss any solutions of that nature.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Excuse me. Mr. Zuzul, you have said that there were human reasons. That at least is the translation, and I would be grateful if you could elaborate a bit. Do you mean personal reasons or -- or what does it mean? I do not understand.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, during that session, and of course I'm telling you about this based on how I remember things to have happened, I think there was quite a severe verbal attack launched, I think, by Mr. Krajisnik against Mr. Izetbegovic. Mr. Izetbegovic looked hurt, if anything, by this sort of approach that took place as part of a round of negotiations. Other than that, there had been a number of situations in which the Serb negotiators took a harsh or even vulgar approach in how they accosted the other delegations. This was one such situation. As to President Tudjman's humanly understandable motives for approaching Izetbegovic thereafter, to be perfectly clear this is just my own personal interpretation of those events.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Now -- I'm told that maybe you should say in English what "Lucki" means. Lucki. Well, the English translation obviously was -- may be incorrect.

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR ZUZUL [Resumed]
utterances.text: [In English] I would also say it was human approach based on empathy.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Empathy. Okay. So in other words, Izetbegovic had been attacked. He's sitting there by himself. Tudjman, being the statesman that he was and a human, went there to comfort another human just to -- after that very difficult and vulgar attack by Krajisnik. Is that basically what it was?

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR ZUZUL [Resumed]
utterances.text: That would be my interpretation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. And it was during that -- that exchange, if you will, when Izetbegovic offered Western Herzegovina and Tudjman rejected it.

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR ZUZUL [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. But the reaction didn't come immediately. We started talking about a number of different things. At one point, the discussion settled on the need for a solution. It was at this time that President Izetbegovic said as follows -- well, I don't think I can quote him with any degree of accuracy, but he made a proposal for Western Herzegovina to secede and join Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. And just one -- I guess let's stay with this for one second. Did -- was there any counter-proposal by President Tudjman and say, "Well, I don't need Western Herzegovina. How about just giving me Neum, and I'll give you that water port that you're looking for," you know, that deep port?

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR ZUZUL [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that time, no proposals were being made by President Tudjman apart from a crystal clear reply to the effect that this was in no way an acceptable solution.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, we're going to go through some documents. I'm going to ask you to keep your answers rather short, and then I'll direct you if I need more amplification. We have quite a few, so we're going to go at a rather rapid clip, but nonetheless I think the information you've provided thus far lays a good foundation for -- for that process. With you, there should be some binders, unless they took them away. Are they are?

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR ZUZUL [Resumed]
utterances.text: [In English] Yes, they are here.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And if you could to binder number 1, and if you could look at the first document, which is 1D 02039.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And incidentally, Your Honours, this is the constitution of the Republic of Croatia. We've seen it before. In fact, we saw it with the very first witness. I mention this because this is a document that is well known to everyone around the court in light of our conversation yesterday, that is.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, let me preface my question by saying we had a witness by the name of Donia that came here. He's an historian who worked for the Prosecution. And in his report -- in his testimony he made references in respect to the Banovina and quoted others or cited others to support his thesis that President Tudjman had aspirations of re-establishing the Banovina Hrvatska boundaries, and both in his report and his testimony he made reference to the constitution. In the preamble, that is. So now I want to go -- I want you to look at this document, 1D 02039, page 1, towards the second to last bullet where it says: "In the establishment of the Banovina of Croatia in 1939 by which Croatian state identity was restored in the Kingdom Of Yugoslavia." Now, if you could please comment on the preamble recognising that, one, you did not draft the constitution but you have been a member of the government and you are from Croatia. You should be aware of the constitution. Can you comment on that and you knew President Tudjman as well?

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR ZUZUL [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Of course I do believe I'm in a position to comment on that. I think I'm sufficiently familiar with Croatia's constitution both as a citizen and as an official. I declare categorically that this interpretation has nothing to do with what is actually contained in the preamble to the Croatian constitution.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Why is that?

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR ZUZUL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Anyone who reads this page without necessarily possessing appropriate legal skills and knowledge must understand that what this is about is the continuity of Croatia's right to sovereignty and not Croatia's right to territory. Were this about territory and not about sovereignty, this would be entirely absurd. In that case, having read the whole thing, Croatia's territory would be somewhere between 10 per cent of its present territory and perhaps 200 per cent of its present territory. It would probably be spilling over into Austria, Hungary, Italy, Slovenia, and perhaps even the Catholic church. If I may just be allowed to furnish an additional explanation as to the importance of the Banovina of Croatia in determining the historic continuity of the Croats' right to statehood. As is well known from history, and that is something that we see mentioned here again, there is a reference to 1918 and the break-up of the Austro-Hungarian monarchy. After the end of World War I and based on the principle of self-determination as defined by Woodrow Wilson, President of the United States, the Croats -- or, rather, Croatia's representatives at the Versailles Conference opted to unite with the Serbs and the Slovenes, thereby constituting the Kingdom of Serbs, Croats, and Slovenes. They did, however, keep their sovereignty and their own parliament. This went on until 1928, when Croat delegates were assassinated in the Yugoslav Assembly. In 1929, the then King of Yugoslavia imposed a constitution on the Croats, defining Yugoslavia as an absolutist monarchy, thereby abolishing any form of sovereignty of the Croatian people. That is why it is so exceptionally important for the idea of continuity as well as its legal foundations that in 1939 following an agreement between the Croatian and Serbian prime ministers, Cvetkovic and Macek, there was a decision by the King to establish the Banovina of Croatia. In territorial terms, this never came to fruition simply because the Second World War started soon after. This was, however, of the essence to Croatia because this gave Croatia back its right to sovereignty, and then documents followed in 1943, 1945, and this period spanned all the way to the 1974 constitution. It is not my intention to pass myself off as a constitutional legal expert. I am, however, convinced that this is the only correct interpretation of the preamble.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. Well, perhaps you might be able to assist us in -- in more concrete ways given that explanation, of course, but in a different context. We had another witness here, John Kenneth Galbraith's son, the famous economist. His son came in. He happened to be the ambassador to Croatia from the United States, Peter Galbraith, and he testified, and he testified that President Tudjman had territorial aspirations and that he believed that Bosnia-Herzegovina would not and should not continue as a sovereign independent state and that a substantial part of Bosnian territory should become the territory of the Republic of Croatia. He indicated that he formed those opinions having met with him on a frequent basis, sometimes even several times a day. He talked about Tudjman being prejudiced against the Muslim people, and he also indicated at one point, he mentioned the fact as further -- as further basis for list supposition that Croatia had a policy of granting Croatian citizens to any ethnic Croat who wanted it, and of course as compared to Bosnia-Herzegovina in this period, you know, that would have been one other way of establishing his territorial ambitions. And I'm quoting -- or this is part from the testimony, Your Honours, for the record. The gentleman testified in open court on September 12, 2006, and passages to basically what I was referring to are from pages 6435, 36, 6427-28, and 6453-54. First let me ask you this, sir: Did you know Peter Galbraith?

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR ZUZUL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And yesterday incidentally, just let me touch on this, you talked about a Contact Group, and as I understand it in the context in which you put it, the Contact Group was established as a result of the failure of the Vance-Owen, Owen-Stoltenberg Plans which were UN-EU coordinated efforts; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR ZUZUL [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was certainly my impression. I think that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: You indicated that one of the members of the Contact Groups was the United States, and my first question is Peter Galbraith, being the American ambassador to Croatia, was he the representative of the United States during those negotiations, the Contact Group, to your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR ZUZUL [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, he was not the representative of the United States in that Contact Group, not the most active representative of the United States. There was one who was specially nominated for that position by President Clinton, and that was Ambassador Charles Redman.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. And again, how well did you know Peter Galbraith?

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR ZUZUL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Quite well, I'd say.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, he indicates that President Tudjman did not want Bosnia and Herzegovina to exist. Is that statement correct in your opinion?

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR ZUZUL [Resumed]
utterances.text: In my opinion, this is an incorrect statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And what about his statement that he wanted to re-establish the borders more or less based on the Banovina?

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR ZUZUL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, I think this is another incorrect statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, he talked about this policy. Policy, and I mention that word, and I underscore it because in some ways, in some circles, in some -- under some circumstances it could give sort of a nefarious notion. Let me ask you this being familiar with the Croatian constitution: Are Croats all over the world, wherever they may be born, do they have the possibility, based on the Croatian constitution, to have a Croatian passport?

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR ZUZUL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Also, do the Croats around the world, wherever it may be, do they have the possibility, based on the Croatian constitution, to serve on the Croatian parliament? I believe it's called Sabor.

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR ZUZUL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And in fact, if I'm not mistaken, are there some seats that are specifically allocated to those Croats because historically speaking there have been Croatian communities throughout the world that have been organised in order to take care of their particular needs?

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR ZUZUL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct. And if I may add to that, because very often it seems to me that this is misinterpreted. Although there is a number of states across the world that allow their citizens who live abroad and work there to participate in the parliamentary life of their respective states, Croatia has had a number of reasons to allow its citizens that privilege, because when the citizens' will was exercised after the democratic elections and when the free Republic of Croatia was established, which was then internationally recognised, one could not and dared not ignore the fact that there was approximately the same number of Croats residing within the territory of Croatia proper as those residing outside of the territory of Croatia. Why was it that this fact should not have been ignored? A number of them had left for economic reasons, but a large number of those Croats had left for political reasons during the time of Communism, and they could not even spend holidays in Croatia or visit their family members. They were not allowed to do so. In other words, when those Croats were given an opportunity to participate in the political life of Croatia, this meant that the injustice was corrected, at least to a certain extent, the injustice that they themselves were not guilty of. They were not to be blamed for that injustice. A provision was introduced that exists in a number of democratic states when this was done.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. I think that --

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR ZUZUL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Likewise -- if I may.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR ZUZUL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that this is very important because your question contained one part that was relative to the possibility of holding a Croatian passport. Maybe you would like me to comment on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Very briefly.

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR ZUZUL [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is true that a large number or a majority of Croats who reside in the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina also have Croatian citizenship and hold Croatian passport because this is provided for by the law -- laws of both Republic of Croatia and Bosnia and Herzegovina. However, based on my knowledge and my information, I believe that I can say that the other state with a number of citizens holding a Croatian passport is the United States of America, and if we followed Ambassador Galbraith's logic, would that mean that Croatia also had aspirations towards the territory of the United States of America? What I'm saying is this is just an absurd claim. These are two things that have nothing whatsoever to do with each other. The right to a passport cannot be interpreted by saying that one nation has territorial aspirations towards the territory of another nation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Thank you for that. Now, we're going to move on to the next document, 1D 02910, and this is a -- a presidential transcript. We've seen it before. It has a D number, Your Honours, because there were some pages that were added. We translated 12 pages, so that would have been the extent of -- this was P 00037. So the 12 added pages would have been the addition to burdening everyone around the court with additional reading. Now, if I may, Your Honours, read from the -- the Prosecution's exhibit list and their 65 ter description of this particular document. It will be my vehicle for the next series of questions. If you have that, sir. Based on -- this is what the Prosecution says: "This transcript shows that Franjo Tudjman had clear territorial ambitions toward Bosnia. The transcript also discusses the deal made between the Serbs and the Croats in Karadjordjevo to divide Bosnia," and their reference is to page 2, 5 to 8, and 38 to 39? First -- first of all, let me ask you do. You have the document with you?

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR ZUZUL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do. I have it in front of me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, this was a presidential transcript that comes from the 7th session of the Supreme State Council, 8 June 1991. First of all, were you present?

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR ZUZUL [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I wasn't present because at that moment I was not politically active at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Have you had an opportunity to -- to go through this presidential transcript?

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR ZUZUL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Excuse me. Just -- just a --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Technical.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Oh, okay. A correction in the transcript. I think it has just disappeared now. The number of the document is not correctly stated. There is an 8 too much, and it might later make it difficult to find it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. It's 1D 02910.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: That's correct. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. And this was Prosecution document P 00037. The only exception is that we've added or translated, I should say, pages 76 to 83, Your Honours, and pages 96 to 100, and you will be able to notice that quite easily if you look at those pages. They're not numbered, but actually you'll see "Unofficial translation" is at the right top part of the page.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: In any event, with that, if we could turn to page 2 just very quickly. I want to focus your attention where it says: "About the sixth meeting of the presidents of the republic." Okay? And then you see: "As you can conclude from the release, certain progress has been made in the talks held so far and that Serbia, which means Montenegro, as well, accepted the basic principle of the establishment of an alliance of sovereign republics." And then it goes on. You also see Izetbegovic's name at the bottom of the page. First of all, if you could help us out a little bit in context because I've noted this is June 8, 1991. What is happening in and around Yugoslavia at that period? And I'm going to ask you to, like, either speak a little faster and shorter so we can go through this material. And I apologise to the translators if they're going to have to labour a little bit more.

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR ZUZUL [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that moment there were almost panic attempts to find a solution to the break-up of Yugoslavia. It was absolutely clear that Yugoslavia could not continue existing in the form that it existed up to then. The collective Presidency stopped functioning. All the republics had their own governments and their own presidents, and in an attempt to find a solution the presidents met on a regular basis, and this is obviously a meeting that took place after the sixth meeting of the of presidents. The international community at that point in time was not showing very much interest in what was happening in Yugoslavia, in -- it did express, however, its position and stated that Yugoslavia should continue existing in one way or another, in one form or another. Two western-most republics of the former Yugoslavia, Slovenia and Croatia, which I dare say were certainly most developed in economic terms and also had managed to develop the most democratic relationships within their respective societies, proposed a model of confederal organisation of Yugoslavia. They did not advocate the break-up of Yugoslavia but, rather, Yugoslavia as a confederation similar to -- to a certain extent to the European Commission or Benelux at its very beginnings. This proposal was drafted by a commission -- a joint commission of Slovenia and Croatia upon the proposal of President Tudjman. The representatives of Serbia and Montenegro rejected that proposal. They did not even want to talk about it and tabled a completely different proposal for the survival of Yugoslavia. According to that proposal, Yugoslavia would have been even more unitarian that it was according to the previous constitution of 1974, and it was absolutely clear that it would be dominated by the Republic of Serbia and Belgrade. The key issue was the position of the president of Bosnia and Herzegovina, Mr. Izetbegovic, and the president Macedonia, Mr. Gligorov. The two of them found it very hard to reach any conclusions or make any decisions. However, when they finally presented their positions, then their positions were much closer to the position of Belgrade and Serbia. Mr. Izetbegovic at one point stated that Bosnia and Herzegovina would be willing and ready to stay with the Rump Yugoslavia. After that and only after that Croatia and Slovenia took steps which would lead to their dissolution and secession from Yugoslavia. At that moment the -- there was something that was very much ignored by the international community but it became very clear already at that point in time that the situation in Yugoslavia would end up in war because the Yugoslav Army was ready for an intervention. At the beginning of 1991, which is now very clear, they had already prepared themselves for a military takeover. On the other hand, everybody was clear that Serbia was getting ready for war. The slogan which became a chapter in one of the internationally recognised books which read "If we don't know how to work, at least we know how to fight," became a -- something that was used by a lot of politicians in Serbia. When you read those things today, then you can see that the predictions of the CIA and other analytical services were that the break-up of Yugoslavia would happen in a war and that this war would be a bloodbath, but at that point in time and -- the international community ignored all that. This, I believe, would give you a general framework within which this discussion took place.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, during those discussions, were there discussions being held to carve up any particular republic, because there are some references here to Karadjordjevo, and that's part of the Prosecution's thesis, that there was a meeting between Tudjman and -- and Milosevic, and at this meeting they had divided to -- they had decided to divide Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR ZUZUL [Resumed]
utterances.text: In this document, I did not find any report about any meetings in Karadjordjevo. I may have omitted this reference, but I don't think it's there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Well, let me just go through one passage, and this would be on page 38. We don't have time to go through this entire document. It would take hours. But just one -- to focus you on this one page, page 38. It says: "The president: All right. Let's wrap up this item. First of all, regarding this proposal, I said there, and the minutes will reflect this, that this proposal by Izetbegovic and Gligorov is actually an attempt to preserve and somewhat bolster the 1974 constitution, basically, that is, Serbia accepted it, but giving it its own interpretation in regards to the creating of an effective democratic federation, and they are sure not to change their position in this regard. Therefore, the solution lies in what was said there, in the -- in the partition of Bosnia and Herzegovina, and if -- and if we achieve that, then we can possibly look for a basis for an alliance of sovereign republics and states. "I think we shall achieve it because this is -- this is equally in the interests of Serbia and Croatia. While the Muslim component has no other exit than to accept the solution, although it will -- it will not be easy to find the solution, but essentially that is it." And then he talks about the next couple -- the next paragraph he talks about the European Community, and then the following paragraph ends with: "Therefore, the question arises whether such a community is at all possible having in mind the economic and other relations in the eastern part of Yugoslavia." Now, if we just looked at this segment in the -- you know, this is just one page out of 163 pages, one might get the impression that what Tudjman is actually suggesting, that Bosnia-Herzegovina should be carved up among at least Serbia and Croatia. Did you get that impression from reading this document?

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR ZUZUL [Resumed]
utterances.text: My impression was that he was just telling about the conversation that he was reporting about, and the conversation took place among the six presidents, and I don't think that this was about any proposals because it transpires from the entire transcript that no such proposal was ever discussed. There was discussion about completely different things, and the thing that was discussed was whether there should be a confederation of all the republics, meaning the six republics that existed at the moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR ZUZUL [Resumed]
utterances.text: For example, he is saying, and I have a Croatian version in front of me, on page 9052 of the Croatian text where President Tudjman says explicitly: "We can start from the position that Croatia may find its own interest in preserving a union of sovereign states." And then we come to the guiding thought in my own interpretation of his whole state -- statesman behaviour. He says: "In this way we should achieve a peaceful separation." And he goes on to say: "A peaceful solution of the Croat-Serb issue on the Croatian territory and the whole -- and the territory as a whole," which means that within the context of the situation that prevailed at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, in quoting -- and there should be page numbers.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: The first page number, Your Honour, was page 43. I'm just as alarmed as you are because I want to make a clear record, and I know you need to follow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: We don't have -- it.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for the Honourable Judge, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think that -- you should have, Your Honour, page 43 of 163.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I have page 9, and the next one is page 38, 39, 40. Okay. So 34 does not figure in this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: You have it? Oh, this is a discrimination against my person, I note because my colleague seems to have it. So I will think of the steps that have to be taken. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well, we apologise. We do massive amounts of copying and printing, and I'll blame it on technology, but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Your apology's accepted.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: This was translated by the Prosecution, Your Honour. I'm not suggesting -- I'm not suggesting that the Prosecutor -- I'm just merely mentioning this -- that this is part of their -- everybody seems --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: As the Court knows it's always the Prosecution's fault.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: -- everybody seems to be so touchy around here.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: What I meant to say was this portion was translated by the Prosecutor. We translated other pages. Therefore they should not have been missing but obviously it was our fault in copying it. So the Prosecutor should just relax a little bit.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, you quoted -- you quoted from another page --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One second. Mr. Witness, I take this opportunity to ask a question linked to what we're talking about. We have a presidential transcript that relates to the 7th session of the Supreme Council of the state of the Republic of Croatia held on the 8th of 1991. Several months ago the Defence challenged those presidential transcripts. You seem to be somebody who may have taken part in one of those meetings, so maybe you will be in a position to solve of some of the problems that we've been faced with. My first question is as follows: Did you personally take part in the Supreme State Council meetings?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. No, Your Honour. Participate in this meeting. I only read the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Maybe not this one, but did you take part in other meetings?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I participated in a number of them, but once I was appointed in 1992.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. In 1992. When you took part in those meetings with President Tudjman, was there somebody who was charged with recording everything that was said by all the participants to these meetings?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Correct, yes. At meetings of this kind there was somebody.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Who was it, a secretary, an employee, somebody specialised?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] These meetings were recorded, and then notes or minutes or transcripts were taken, and as far as I know there were a few professional typists, ladies, who did that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. You have by your answers given authenticity to those transcripts.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Honourable Judge --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: At some point today hopefully we'll get to a transcript where Mr. Zuzul is mentioned. There is an exchange which we will see he did not participate in. So authenticity is one thing, accuracy is another, and we'll get to that at some point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. But I believe the witness wanted to say something else.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It indeed happened in the way Mr. Karnavas described. As I am reading these transcripts, and this is my first opportunity to read them carefully, I have been able to convince myself that they contain errors, misidentification of person, misinterpretation of their words. And since I know the conditions under which the recordings were made were far, far from ideal, I'm not surprised to see those errors, but it is my personal impression that every transcript has to be checked and re-checked because of those errors, and I'm going to be able to give you my own example to illustrate one of the errors that are contained in one of those transcripts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Judge Trechsel, did we solve your problem? Okay. Thank you. And we apologise again. And it was no fault of the Prosecution's, so they shouldn't -- I just want to make sure that there's not shifting the blame on anyone.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, I noticed that earlier that one of your answers, you used the word "unitarian," and -- and I see that on page -- one of the pages that we translated which would have been -- it should be page 46, 47, 48, 49 -- I mean, 96, 97, 98, 99, I believe right around there. It says here: "Therefore it is necessary that we cooperate until all possibilities are exhausted and that we create both in principle and personally the best possible relations because that is in our interest, interest of the army and of individuals, but of course we will not be silent about -- we will not be silent about such cases. We will present them as an existence of those elements and dogmatic Communist and unitarian Greater Serbia as they do exist in society not only within the army but also in all state -- in all strata of the society as well as extremists among us which hinder achieving a political solution." If you could -- I just want to dwell a little bit on this unitarian Greater Serbia. What is meant by that, because we've heard the term "unitary government." Now we have a variation of that word, "unitarian." What was your understanding of that in the context of which we're speaking of, because it might assist us.

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR ZUZUL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, for all of us who group up in Yugoslavia the meaning of the term "unitary" was something that we knew from our everyday lives. It was not something that was learned from constitutional practice, because the more the federal state became unitary or unitaristic the less rights were enjoyed by the republics. Yugoslavia's history is the history of defining unitary versus federal system. In this particular paragraph that you've just quoted, President Tudjman, in my opinion, is referring to something that had already happened in Serbia by that time. While Yugoslavia existed, in 1974 constitution there was the federal system, but Serbia had two autonomous provinces under this constitution, Vojvodina and Kosovo. At the time when this is being discussed, Serbia had already rescinded the right to the autonomy in both those districts, especially in Kosovo, and from that time until the recent time when Kosovo declared its independence as a state and was recognised as such this was the period when there was the Kosovo crisis, and President Tudjman and all the other participants were quite familiar with this crisis. So he is talking about this unitary Serbia, Serbia that is rescinding all rights to autonomy and urges the creation of a Yugoslavia that would, it is quite clear, be set up not on the federal principles, not on confederal principles, but on unitary principles. It would be in Serbia's way. I think that's what this paragraphs actually all about.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. We're going to move on to this next document because we're running a little bit behind. So if we could go to 1D 00894. This is from "Balkan Odyssey." This is a document that we've seen before. In fact we've seen these pages, again no additional reading for anyone around the court. No surprise. But I want to point out one thing and have you comment on it. On chapter 2 Lord Owen in his book says, bottom of the first -- of the second paragraph on the first page: "The Netherlands had the EC Presidency from the outbreak of the war in July until December 1991, and in consequence of my visit to The Hague, I discovered that on 13 July 1991, when the Slovenian and Croatian declarations of independence were just eighteen days old, the Dutch government had suggested to the other EC members states that the option of agreed changes to some of the internal borders between the Yugoslavian republic might be explored." Now, I ask you to think about this only because the issue of changing of the borders have come up. From your experiences were you aware of any of the international negotiators exploring possibilities, that is initiating, because I think that's the word, initiating possibilities of changing of borders? And I mention this because of the Prosecution's theory of joint criminal enterprise that Croatia was initiating this process of changing borders?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour. I'm sorry to intervene. I'm waiting for my microphone. Thank you very much. Your Honour, I'm mindful that the Chamber, or at least some members of the Chamber, do not like many interventions from counsel, and I've been quiet all day for the most part I think with one exception, but I am going to object and continue to object. There is no reason on this basis; that is, there is no reason for Mr. Karnavas to make speeches in connection with his questions and characterise them as this is what the Prosecution says. This is the Prosecution's theory of the case. It is a form of coaching, Your Honour. It's the key words to the witness to say this is what the Prosecution says, so I'm telling you now this is what you, the witness, are supposed to disagree with. Mr. Karnavas can simply ask non-leading questions to the witness. Were you in such a meeting at this day? Tell us what happened. Did you talk to Izetbegovic about this subject? What did he say? Were you at this meeting or not? No, I wasn't. But there is no reason for constant speeches or characterisations of this is what the Prosecution says, so now I'm telling you, Mr. Witness, I want you, I'm expecting you to say the opposite. It's a form of coaching. We object to it. While I'm on my feet, while I'm on my feet, number two, number two, I want to make the record clear, and I'll say why, in terms of the transcripts, in the last transcript, the presidential transcript that we were looking at, and this is not directed at Mr. Karnavas or the Defence at all, but I just want the record to be clear on something because I know statements have been made in the Croatian press, statements have been made in the Croatian media that the Prosecution, for example, used only -- offered bits and pieces or excerpts of the presidential transcripts that the Prosecution tendered into evidence. As the Chamber knows, that's not the case. The Prosecution's position was we tendered the entire transcript, top to bottom, with the exception of a very few where they were long transcripts and it was very clear to any reader that the last 80 pages had absolutely nothing to do with anything at issue in this case, whether to enter into a free trade agreement with China, I don't think we needed 80 pages on that. With those kind of exceptions, we tendered every single page of every single transcript, and so when the Croatian media writes its article tomorrow about the hearing today that says, well, Mr. Karnavas had to add other excerpts because the Prosecution had not played fairly, I just want it to be clear, the Prosecution offered the entire transcripts, and it was the Chamber that only decided to accept bits and pieces.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, with regard to the media, that's not the Trial Chamber's problem. We're not going to issue our judgement based on some press cuttings. That's one thing. That's your problem, not ours. However, with regard to the objection you've just raised. Mr. Karnavas, I believe that the objection is in part justified. Initially you should have asked the witness whether he had any knowledge of possible changes within the internal borders, and he could have said yes, no, and then you could have asked him to look at what Lord Owen said in his book. Based on that, he would have said, yes, indeed. Then third step, you can say, "The Prosecution in its indictment claims this and that. Do you agree or not?" Otherwise, you should have preempt or you lead the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Very well, Mr. President, but I do want to take exception to the Prosecution's characterisation that I'm coaching the witness. First of all, we had a narrative. We had a narrative where we talked about changing of borders or swapping. We had a narrative where it was Izetbegovic that offered part of Herzegovina. We had a narrative where it was Izetbegovic that signed an agreement to allow half of Bosnia to be carved away, so it's not as if I'm coaching the witness, but I take -- I take your observations and I will modify my -- my technique.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Concerning this, sir, do you have any knowledge with respect to international negotiators proposing the possibility at least that they should explore the alteration of the borders within Yugoslavia made up -- that separated the republics?

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR ZUZUL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that the option of peaceful changing of the borders was mentioned in several international documents. Lord Owen writes about that at several places in his book. This is one of those places. In the first stage of the work of the conference for the former Yugoslavia, that was always on the table as an option, so voluntary changing of the borders in accordance with the mutual agreement. After all, the case that I described yesterday was initiated by the representatives of the international community, possible territory swaps between Croatia and Serbia. So I am aware of the fact that there was such thinking, and I know that it was mentioned in several international documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Now we move to the next document and that would be 1D 00893. I think we've seen this document as well. So without adding too much commentary, I do want to point out that this was a document that is familiar to everyone here. Now, if we can look at this. This is the European Community conference. We have a draft convention. It mentions Lord Carrington, and there's a treaty proposal. I will ask you to first focus on Article 1 where it talks about new relations between the republics, and under 1(c) common state of equal republics for those republics which wish to remain in a common state. Under (f), recognition of the independence within the existing borders unless otherwise agreed. I then want you to focus on page 16, the section called special status, which says in addition areas in which persons belonging to a national or ethnic group form a majority shall enjoy a special status of autonomy, and it talks about the right to use national emblems, educational system, et cetera. First of all, are you familiar with this document?

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR ZUZUL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I am familiar with it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. And to your knowledge this is what was being discussed at the time?

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR ZUZUL [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was the framework for the debate and for the thinking in the period between 1991 and the London conference which took place in 1992, because this was, in fact, the only official document produced by the international community.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, we see from the very -- the preamble, we see that this is November -- 1 -- we see it was November 1991. What is happening in Croatia at that point in time?

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR ZUZUL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Immediately before this, on the 8th of October, Croatia made its decision to become independent, and in the international sphere Croatia was trying to achieve international recognition based, among other things, on this document as a state within its borders, and soon after this document was produced Croatia was indeed recognised, first unofficially by Germany. The recognition was then postponed until mid-January 1992. This was when the European states followed the Vatican, the Holy See, and recognised Croatia within its existing borders. Internally in Croatia at the time the war escalated. The Yugoslav army attacked from several sides, and as I said yesterday, large areas of Croatia were occupied and Croatia was for all intents and purposes cut in two.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, if we go to the next document, P 00089. It's a Prosecution document. We've seen this before. It's been talked about quite a bit by various witnesses, and it's been referenced, in fact, by some in their works. This is 27 December 1991. You more or less told us politically what is happening and physically what is happening in Croatia. First let me begin by asking have you read this presidential transcript?

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR ZUZUL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Were you present --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I'm sorry, could you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: The number is clear. In which folder is it? We have five.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well, all these documents are in a chronological order, so if you -- the number. So it would be -- you would need to go to the next binder. So number 1, number 2 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Number 2.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Yep. We have it that way. If I do go out of order, I'll make sure to give everybody the heads-up. I only have three binders. That's why, so ...

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Anyway, while we're looking for those, just some preliminary questions. Were you present during this discussion?

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR ZUZUL [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I was not.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, just to touch on a couple of points. First let me ask you: Given your position and your involvement in the various events, do you feel competent that you might be able to discuss certain contents in this document?

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR ZUZUL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think yes. I think I can. I think I can give you some elements regarding the interpretation of this document, and quite by coincidence after I read this document now for the first time, perhaps I can provide some additional information that might shed light on the circumstances, the time when this was going on.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Well --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour, excuse me again --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour, in light of what was just said, I'm going to object to this kind of just simply tell us your interpretation of the document, the document the witness has no personal knowledge of. He was not present at the meeting. He's told us that. And, you know, this is what Mr. Karnavas -- a word Mr. Karnavas himself likes to use. This is just spin. I've got a witness here from the Tudjman government, and I'm going to ask him to give his spin on this material, and that's all it is. I have no objection if -- if he asks about a specific question about something that may have a technical meaning, something -- a moment ago he said something, what would "unitary" mean. I didn't object to that. I think probably that's something the witness might be able to assist us with. But to simply take a presidential transcript of a meeting where the witness was not involved, he wasn't even in government at that time to my knowledge - this is December 1991 - and just simply put it before the witness, "Witness, what do you think about this? What's your spin on this?" And that's all this is. That's all it is. Objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. I've heard the objection loud and clear, and may I respond. I'll be measured. The Prosecutor brought in Donia, someone who got a degree in the United States on 19th century intellectual Muslims in Sarajevo, had a career in banking -- or in financing. Twenty-some years later, writes a book with very few footnotes and then becomes a "Prosecution expert," reads this, cites it. Ribicic, Constitutional Judge in Slovenia, writes a book supposedly analysing the laws, the basis of Herceg-Bosna, does a constitutional analysis, and if you look at the portions and you look at the transcript, and by the way I did look at it before coming here today, but if you look at it - I'm afraid I didn't bring it in because of time - you will see that I referenced the part where he gets to say, "Once I read this particular transcript, I changed my opinion." And then if you recall, there was a heated exchange where even you, Judge Trechsel, intervene at one point because I said, well, what about all these other transcripts. You know, and he said, well, he didn't read them, and of course my position at that point was that his report should be stricken from the record because obviously that report was written when he only looked at one particular transcript and not the others, at which point as I recall, Judge Trechsel, you indicated well, you know, he could spend his lifetime reading all this stuff or that could be supplemented, but be that as it may, be that as it may, the point that I'm trying to make is this: When the Prosecution wants to have somebody who wasn't present and take one sliver out of a presidential transcript, and I dare say he wasn't quite correct when he said earlier that he's tendered everything. He's only translated portions, translated portions, so tendering is one thing. Translating is another, so if you only have two or three passages of 160 pages or whatever, he has it. But be that as it may, he brings in outsiders, not participants, to comment, to opine, and then he uses that as the foundation in establishing the joint criminal enterprise, and the first time I bring in someone who is aware of the events, and had Mr. Scott listened because he got a little excited there and was ready for his objection, but he didn't listen to the end of Mr. Zuzul's answer, which was having read that, he's able to comment on certain things. So he got a little excited, didn't listen to the whole answer, and now here we are wasting valuable time. But I want to point that out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. We are right. We are losing and wasting time. You're both right. You know, Mr. Karnavas, you should, in order to avoid this objection because you are an experienced professional and you know how to do it, initially you should have told

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: "During the proofing session, we both looked at this document, P 89, 160 pages long, and we mentioned this and that page. Expert Donia in his report said this and that. Could you, Witness, enlighten the Trial Chamber on specific points," because then the Prosecutor would not have anything to object to.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Very well, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: If I may add a point. It strikes me that you are comparing witnesses, your witness here --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: -- to experts brought by the Prosecution, and I don't think that is really quite equitable. An expert is asked to give opinions on matters. A witness is asked to speak about facts that he has witnessed, and the question you put to your witness, in my view, is totally a question for an expert. Now, your witness has not been presented as an expert. We do not have any credentials like we have for an expert, and I think there's a little problem here.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well, let me respond to that because I beg to differ with you significantly. Ribicic read law. That's what he did. Now, what makes him an expert to take a presidential transcript and to say based on this he's making a constitutional analysis? And just because we call somebody an expert doesn't make him an expert. Donia worked for the Prosecution, and I dare say in my 25 years of working in this business, I'm entitled to ask a layperson to provide expert testimony if they're capable of doing that. So I've asked -- that was -- that was a foundational question. Having read it, is he able to comment on it? He is an expert in a sense even though a fact witness in some ways because he spent time over there. He was with President Tudjman. He knew the events. He represented the government. You're shaking your head, but that's the fact. Now, what I would do -- what I would ask -- what I would ask, Judge Trechsel, is that -- that you begin registering your objections on the record because it seems to me that at this point, at this point, it is curtailing my defence. Not only am I limited in time, now I'm being limited in scope, as well, and I don't think I agree with your analysis, but if that's the case I would like a clear record exactly, and give me -- give me the scope. Tell me how you want me to do it, so maybe I make submissions for an interlocutory appeal, but at this point I must say, with your interpretation I wholly disagree, especially when we say that we're practising before professional Judges, especially because of that, and we can't have it both ways, but I dare say that the gentleman can comment because he was there and he knows the circumstances, and if I was allowed to ask those questions that I wanted to ask, you would see. Now, how much weight you give to that, that's a different story, but I think I have -- I was laying the predicate that would allow me to ask those questions because I wasn't asking him for an expert opinion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Well, you have challenged me, and I will give you an answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I'm not making an objection. I'm just recalling that we have witnesses, according to the Rules of Procedure, and we have experts, and it is news to me that -- that they are the same and that you can switch and take the expert as a witness and the witness as an expert if it pleases you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: But maybe I'm wrong on this.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, let me just -- I don't want to have a philosophical or legal debate, but let's just say hypothetically speaking, hypothetically speaking I brought in as a fact witness a general. Now, by virtue of his position, by virtue of his knowledge, by virtue of his experience, is not that general able, capable, willing, if I asked the question, to answer technical questions regarding military matters that are outside what he has observed? Of course. Do I need to qualify him as an expert? Of course not. If it's relevant I should be able to ask that question. Now, it shouldn't be -- I shouldn't be trying to sabotage the Prosecution, but I could certainly ask him technical questions. It comes within that. Let's just say that I have a regular witness, and I'm asking him if he can identify somebody's voice like you have these recordings. If I can lay the foundation that that individual does recognise the person's voice because he's heard it a hundred times on the telephone, in a sense that person is giving expert testimony because he's capable of identifying the voice. So that's how you can. I'm not bringing this gentleman in as an expert nor was my questioning eliciting expert testimony. I was asking him to opine on what he was able to glean from reading this, and had -- had we been allowed, he would have been able -- he's indicated that after reading this he has some personal experience of which he can discuss certain matters. That's not an expert.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Before the break, yes, Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I've been patient and hopefully this will give Mr. Karnavas a chance to take a breath. I fully agree with what Judge Trechsel said and that was in my notes, and Judge Trechsel you beat me to it and good for you for that. This is now -- this is now -- the witness is now being tendered as an expert. That's the difference between the witnesses -- the Prosecution witnesses that Mr. Karnavas cites and this witness. And I might add in light of the issues that were raised yesterday, we can add now to the deficiencies the lack of an expert report. We don't have a statement. We don't have an adequate summary. We don't have notice of an expert. We don't have an expert report. So we just got a free-ranging witness here, a member of the Tudjman government, who can just come in and give his views about anything that Mr. Karnavas wants to ask him about. Now, that is not appropriate. You cannot simply, with all due respect to this Chamber, all of whom I have great respect for, you cannot appeal every time to say it's professional Judges as if that means there are no rules. Yes, you are professional Judges. There are still Rules of Procedure and rules of evidence that should be followed and just to say it's professional Judges, no holds barred, everything is fair, you can do whatever you want, is not correct. These are -- further these are not technical matters. I added a moment ago -- I asked a moment -- I made the comment a moment ago: If someone says it was a term of art and a witness could say, "Well, I'm a general and I happen to know that when that term is used this is what it means." These are not technical matters. These are clearly political matters, political matters of the most direct kind. I'm going to give you my political interpretation on these events, and I've never -- I wasn't at the meeting, I've never seen this before, but now that I've read it I'm going to give you my political interpretation of events and that's all we're getting, Your Honour, and I we do object and I'm going to continue to object to this kind of testimony.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well Your Honour -- Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One moment. Let me give my own opinion. First of all, I do not agree with what Mr. Scott has just said. We are here with a witness who was a Minister of Foreign Affairs in Croatia, who was the representative of Croatia in international negotiations, who also participated in the work related to the Vance-Owen Plan. The Defence counsel is examining the witness on issues related to borders, to meetings between Tudjman and other individuals with regard to these geopolitical problems. Without the witness being an expert but in his field of foreign affairs, he's no doubt an expert because if you have a minister of foreign affairs who would not be able to address issues of foreign affairs, where are the experts, then? And I do remind you that the Trial Chamber is made up of two former ambassadors among the Judges, and I believe that the Defence are entitled to ask questions of the witness. The only residual issue that may remain is to make sure that the questions as they are asked are not leading because we're dealing here with a common law procedure. So as the chief examiner, he should not put leading questions. So that would be a cause for objections by the Prosecution. But, I mean, if he asked questions that could challenge the case of the Prosecutor, that's another matter. There should not be automatically objections if the Prosecution's case is being challenged. We have just spent about half an hour on procedural matters whereas I and I believe my colleagues, too, are interested in the substance of the case. We are going to break for 20 minutes, and we shall resume thereafter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The hearing is resumed. Mr. Karnavas, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Mr. Zuzul, if you could turn to page 27 of this particular document. We're still on P 00089, 27 December 1991, and I'm going to read a portion here, and I'm going ask you if you're able to comment on it. It says here "the president," so that would be President Tudjman. I'm going to go to the bottom of the page first. It says, "There are numerous indicators that, you see, that America would gladly accept Serbia in the policing role against the Muslims to forestall the establishment of a Muslim state in Europe." Now, throughout those years that you were involved in the various positions that you held, was that ever a concern, that is, that they might be -- that the US or other countries, Western countries, were reluctant to see the establishment of a Muslim state in Europe? And that would be, of course, part of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR ZUZUL [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was certainly what President Tudjman had in mind. He believed there was concern both in America and in some of Europe's countries about the possibility to establish a pure Muslim state in Europe.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. At this point in time, 27 December 1991, had Croatia recognised Bosnia and Herzegovina's independence? This is December 27, 1991. Or I should put -- I should rephrase it. Had Bosnia and Herzegovina opted for independence at that point in time?

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR ZUZUL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe they were preparing for independence, but no international recognition had been granted by this time. I'm certain about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, further down -- in the next page, page 28, I'm just going to hit this rather quickly, certain passages, it says, "Izetbegovic, even Stipe may recall," and I suspect that he's talking about Stipe Mesic, "once openly said that he would favour a solution whereby Slovenia would go. Croatia would have somewhat more, and Bosnia would be more closely associated with Serbia. The establishment of borders, will we set up border crossings between Croatia and Herzegovina so that a Croat from Herzegovina may not go to his own Croatia or Croat from here may not go there? Shall we set up customs office? Shall we set up customs? Shall we make it so that one has to, as the government has already issued and rightly so, an order that petrol may be sold and so on? Shall we -- shall we a currency in the end," as written, "all this together? These are the problems that arise in everyday administrative and legislative sense, which establish new relationships which would be unbearable among according to this view, not only for Croatia in view of the shape of its borders but also for the Croatian part of the Herzegovina and Bosnian territory. "In addition, if Bosnia and Herzegovina was to remain whole, what are Croatia's prospects there?" If we go down to the -- to the next paragraph. "During the talks under these circumstances, we supported the position of preserving a sovereign Bosnia and Herzegovina precisely because the Greater Serbia policy raised the issue of Serbian areas in Croatia. "Therefore, in such circumstances, it would have been politically unwise for us to raise the issue of demarcation of borders in Bosnia and Herzegovina otherwise. However, if you recall as early as 1989, we said in our delegation the historic HDZ declaration" I'm sorry, "the historic HDZ declaration that we were for a sovereign Bosnia and Herzegovina unless its existence came into question because in that case, in view of the interests of the Croatian people, we have to raise the issue of Croatian borders." First of all, let me ask you this: By this point this time were you a member of -- of HDZ? We're talking December.

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR ZUZUL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I became a member in October that year, but I was just an ordinary member.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And how much, if any, of Croatia's territory had been occupied or was under attack at that point in time?

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR ZUZUL [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that point in time virtually a third of Croatia's territory had been occupied already. Vukovar had fallen. Eastern Slavonia was under occupation, and on the 10th of September the siege of Dubrovnik and attacks on the town began. Dubrovnik was now under siege, and at this time was being subjected to heavy gunfire.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: In light of your background, experience, and knowledge, are you able to decipher, if you would, where on page 28 President Tudjman says: "Izetbegovic, even Stipe may recall, once openly said that he would favour a solution whereby Slovenia would go, Croatia would have somewhat more and Bosnia would be more closely associated with Serbia"?

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR ZUZUL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, indeed. That's what I was talking about earlier on. There were clear indicia as far as a solution for the former Yugoslavia was concerned. The Muslim leadership had certain inclinations in favour of Serbia, and I think Izetbegovic didn't hold that back. I think he said as much even when the attacks on Bosnia and Herzegovina were first being launched. Even prior to this there were villages in Dubrovnik's hinterland, in Eastern Herzegovina that had already been attacked by the JNA already and had been destroyed in their entirety.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: What kind of army did Croatia have at the time?

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR ZUZUL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Croatia had already managed to set up a proper army. We established defence lines and put a stop to any further advances by the JNA. However, at the time it was still unable to defend its territory in its entirety. I think I did spend a great deal of time discussing that yesterday. Now, however, just before the turn of the year in 1992, the greatest danger was the Dubrovnik situation and the possibility that Dubrovnik might fall, as well as the entire area. Not just the area around Dubrovnik but, rather, the city of Dubrovnik itself as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Let me -- let me just walk you step by step on this now. At this point in time, is the -- are the JNA forces in Bosnia and Herzegovina, and, if so, where are they?

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR ZUZUL [Resumed]
utterances.text: There is no doubt that they were there. I don't think anybody had asked them by this time to leave Bosnia and Herzegovina officially. I think didn't that happened until sometime later, but it's quite certain that there were JNA units in Bosnia and Herzegovina. It is quite certain that they were launching attacks on the republic of Croatia from there. I mentioned several times the area around Dubrovnik and the forces that were arriving from Herzegovina, from Montenegro. These JNA forces were attacking Dubrovnik, but there were attacks like that going on in the Posavina area, as well, and just north of Knin. There were several areas in which the JNA were carrying out attacks from Bosnian territory.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. And yesterday you told us that you had joined the army. At that point in time, where -- were you in the army or working for the department of defence?

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR ZUZUL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was partly in the Croatian army at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. And were you stationed in anyplace in particular?

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR ZUZUL [Resumed]
utterances.text: We were stationed in Zagreb, but it was precisely around this time that I and my colleagues travelled south to Dubrovnik, our intention being to reach Dubrovnik. However, that wasn't possible. Perhaps a month and a half before this, I had been to the Opuzen area. I said that I might have some additional explanations that might shed light on the background of this meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Let me -- let me just lead you step by step because before we get there, I just want to make sure that I'm crystal clear. It's December 1991. Croatia has declared its independence. Croatia is under attack by the JNA. The JNA is staging attacks using Bosnian -- from the Bosnia and Herzegovinian territory, and as I understand yesterday from your testimony, Bosnia and Herzegovina did nothing to stop it. Perhaps it could not do anything. Let me ask you this question based on this background: What -- let me make sure I phrase it in a way that it can be answered in a non-leading fashion. Were there discussions with respect to Bosnia and Herzegovina's viability as a state and, if so, can you please tell us? And we're talking about historically that period in time because we know that Bosnia-Herzegovina has not yet declared its independence, but at that point.

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR ZUZUL [Resumed]
utterances.text: There probably were, but in the context of defending Croatia there was no one to raise this with in Bosnia and Herzegovina as a serious issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR ZUZUL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I will try to be more specific. I'm talking about the leaders of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Okay. And did -- as far as you know, and I'm asking you -- maybe you didn't know back at the time, that is back in December, but thereafter did you ever learn, given your experience and the positions that you held, what Izetbegovic's position was at that point in time? Did you ever come out and expressly say, "We are for independence. We are against Yugoslavia. We want this or that"? Was there ever some sort of a public expression which we could look at and identifiably know exactly where that man, given his position and his responsibility, stood at at the time?

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR ZUZUL [Resumed]
utterances.text: His position as to the future of Bosnia and Herzegovina was not entirely clear. He said he had a preference for Belgrade's solution. As far as war was concerned, his position unfortunately was clear. He said this wasn't their war and that he had no desire to interfere. If we try to interpret this, and we look at transcript one, the Croatian representatives, he talks about his own meeting with General Kadijevic, Mr. Kljuic's specifically. His conviction is not only that the army would not attack Bosnia and Herzegovina but, rather, that the army would be allowing political parties to take control in Bosnia and Herzegovina. We know now that this was quite gullible as a line of reasoning since the war had already begun, a war true and proper.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, to make sure that we fully understand, who is Mr. Kadijevic?

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR ZUZUL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Kadijevic was at the time the defence minister of a disintegrating Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. And when you say "army," which army are we talking about?

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR ZUZUL [Resumed]
utterances.text: [In English] Yugoslav People's Army, JNA.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Just to make sure I'm crystal clear, because I'm just a little confused here, at this period of time we see an exchange between Tudjman and Kljuic. Of course we all knew because Kljuic was here that at the time he was president of the HDZ. And what exactly is Kljuic saying to Tudjman so we are -- and be as precise as you can so we can understand that.

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR ZUZUL [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The transcript is quite long. We see Kljuic as president of Bosnia and Herzegovina's HDZ, and we realise that he had just talked to General Kadijevic. Tudjman asked him an explicit question; namely, whether he had talked to Izetbegovic and Karadzic, who were then the political leaders of the other two ethnicities in Bosnia and Herzegovina. It appeared clear that he had not talked to them. He, much like Izetbegovic, still believed, at least that's how it comes across to me, that the JNA could be part of a solution and not one of the sources of crisis. Apart from Kljuic, there was a large delegation of Bosnia and Herzegovina's Croats attending this meeting.
