utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I just want to make sure. I don't want to get into the whole debate, but this issue here is very important. Kljuic is under discussion with Kadijevic, and -- because you said that they were somewhat naive or gullible, gullible, I believe the word was, I think that's the part that we want to be crystal clear, because we know in context that Croatia is being attacked from Bosnia and Herzegovina, and now we have the highest Croat representative, and he's saying words, at least if I understand you, that they think that they can do business with the JNA, that is, Sarajevo government. So could you please tell us what is it that is being said in that, because you understand the events better than we do.

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR ZUZUL [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is precisely what I was about to point out. On the one hand, we have Mr. Kljuic; and on the other, Mr. Kljuic who is saying just what I've been telling you about. That's my impression, and I think you've just summed it up. That was his conviction. He said he still believed that an agreement could be reached, even an agreement with the Yugoslav Army. On the other hand, there were a group of Croats from Bosnia and Herzegovina on their way to see President Tudjman, the president of Croatia, with their own proposals, a whole list of those, in fact, that were strikingly different from what Kljuic was suggesting at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, in this transcript we see the name of Mate Boban. At that point in time, did you know him?

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR ZUZUL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did. I had known him for quite some time before the war erupted. I can't say I knew him well. He was older than me. I grew up in a small town call Imotski, however, and Mr. Boban worked there. He was the manager of one of the major companies based in the area. It was called Napredak. That was when I made his acquaintance. During the war, however, just before the developments that I have now been discussing, I had been directly in touch with Mr. Boban.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, I believe you wanted to say something earlier, and I cut you off of a little bit --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PRANDLER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karnavas. I apologise for interrupting you, but since we have been dealing with the document here, with the minutes of this meeting under the chairmanship of the President Franjo Tudjman, I would like to take this opportunity, not tomorrow when the Judges are supposed to ask questions, to ask the witness about a particular point since we are here at the document and you have already -- I mean, Mr. Karnavas, you have already asked several questions about the document, pages 28, I believe, and others. And now I would like to address myself to the -- to page 31, 31, of this very document, that is the document 00089, I believe. And 31, you -- concerning the future of Bosnia and Herzegovina, there are interesting remarks. Let me quote or -- it's a long quotation. President Tudjman said: "In other words, the sovereignty of Bosnia in the present circumstances from the Croatian standpoint is such that not only do we not have to advocate it, we must not even raise the issue openly. However, why not accept this offer of demarcation -- " the demarcation which would have demarcated into three parts Bosnia and Herzegovina, and of course it would offered, as we recall, we spoke about it this morning, and I continue now with the quotation. "However, why not accept this offer of demarcation when it is in the interest of the Croatian people, the Croatian people here in this republic, and the Croatian people in Bosnia and Herzegovina, because I do not see a single reason, a single serious reason, against it. Moreover, in the talks I -- that I personally conducted with Izetbegovic and Milosevic, in addition one of our people in Bosnia drafted a proposal for demarcation, whereby the Croatian areas and those that you have included in this community of Herceg-Bosna and in the community of Croatian Posavina, in the event of demarcation, Croatia wouldn't get not only those two communities, Croatia would not only get those two communities but also for geopolitical reasons Cazinska and Bihacka Krajina, which would satisfy almost ideally the Croatian national interests, not only present but also for the future and then from the remaining areas." End of the quotation. And now my question is to Mr. Zuzul. If -- how would you in a way view this excerpt of the transcript as far as the position, of course it was in late 1991, position of President Tudjman concerning the future of Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] First of all, I thank you, Your Honour. May I say this isn't just because I was part of Tudjman's cabinet, which I was. It is because I wished to tell the truth, the truth that I saw and the way I saw it. I want to tell you how I think about this when I think about it. I think one thing that this transcript shows is one of the principles -- or, rather, all of the principles that Tudjman was applying whenever he thought about the future. The first thing being protecting Croatia's borders, the second thing being protecting the rights of the Croatian people -- the rights of the Croatian people in Bosnia and Herzegovina, and the third thing being putting a stop to the war. When he discusses this, what he actually means is a division within Bosnia and Herzegovina, but this is what I was trying to point out having read the transcript: Tudjman is facing a proposal made by a delegation of Croats from Bosnia and Herzegovina. The proposal was formulated as a set of 19 issues or items. If you look at item 27 -- or, rather, page 27, that Tudjman was not familiar with those conclusions. He did, however, show respect to this group of Croats who came to see him, and I can comment why, if you like. And he responds as to why he believed that the only solution acceptable, and this is earlier on before the negotiations, was a demarcation within the borders of Bosnia and Herzegovina. Regardless of the fact that President Tudjman at the time knew that such a response was not likely to satisfy everyone since there were people around who really believed that some parts of Bosnia and Herzegovina's territory should be annexed by Croatia, since some people sincerely believed at the time that this was the only direction that this moment in history could possibly take, nevertheless we have those opinions on the one hand and President Tudjman's opinions in his capacity as president on the other, and I think the distinction between the two is perfectly clear. If I may just add something based on my own knowledge of the situation and something specific about Mr. Boban. It is due to a sheer coincidence that I know about the following: Not long before this President Tudjman had first been in touch with Mr. Boban in a way that illustrated the totality of what was going on at the time. I can testify to this based on my own direct experience. I was part of the Croatian army, as I have pointed out already, and we were headed for Dubrovnik, I along with several of my other colleagues, university lecturers. We were trying to contribute to the defence effort. We reached Opuzen and realised that the situation was bordering on sheer panic. The Croatian army, which was only in the process of being organised, was simply unable to defend the area. They were short on manpower and equipment. We spoke to the command there, and someone raised the following issue: What about the Croats from Herzegovina? It was a well-known fact that many of those had volunteered to the Croatian army in order to defend Croatia. Among our group, representatives of the Croatian army from Zagreb, there was also Mr. Marinko Boban. In Croatia, his reputation is due to the fact that he is the father of probably the most famous Croatian football player ever, Zvonimir Boban. A little indiscretion, if I may. I was travelling with Marinko Boban in a car that his son had received as a gift from his own football club, FC Milan. That's what the times were like. There is nothing else I can say. We were trying to set up some sort of defence. At one point in time, someone at the table had raised the following issue: Maybe Boban would be able to help. Maybe he could make available some volunteers. He might give us a hand. The person they meant was Mato Boban, who had by this time had been appointed to lead the Croats in Herzegovina -- or, rather, that part of Bosnia and Herzegovina. We made a call to President Tudjman. Following our conversation, I understood that he knew about Mate Boban but that they had never met. Just to be specific about the time line, I'm talking about late October, possibly early November. So this is just under two months before the Zagreb meeting. Nevertheless, President Tudjman agreed that Mr. Marinko Boban should travel to Herzegovina, of which he, too, was a native, and that he should talk to his relative Mate Boban and ask him if he could help with defending Dubrovnik. Marinko Boban returned the same night late - it was well past midnight - to inform us that Mate Boban had made a promise to secure an entire battalion of volunteers who would be prepared to defend and attack the JNA in Herzegovina. Those volunteers were Croats, but they were Croats from Bosnia and Herzegovina. Marinko Boban later told me and President Tudjman that this really occurred, that this materialised. Several days later, a group of Croat volunteers from Herzegovina crossed to Eastern Herzegovina, Dubrovnik's hinterland, and this was possibly one of the key factors in the defence of Dubrovnik and the eventual success in defending the city. I'm talking about telling the truth as I saw it. Why did I deem it important to point out this very fact and to address this particular meeting? President Tudjman knows that he not only enjoys the political support of the Croats from Herzegovina. He also knows that he needs them in order to do something that constituted one of the most important strategic goals at the time, which was to defend Dubrovnik. He pays his respect to them at that meeting. He values their presence. It wasn't a matter of agreeing or disagreeing with what they were actually saying. He knew that they were the only ones at the time capable of carrying this extra burden of defence. I don't know whether between the episode that I've just described and the meeting there was any actual communication between President Tudjman and Mr. Boban. I simply don't know. I do, however, believe, Your Honours, that if we place this against that sort of a background then reading the entire transcript is cast in an entirely different light. These proposals are being made but not by President Tudjman. He's discussing these proposals. He's discussing these proposals with people that he respects, with people who are members of the same political party. They respected him in political terms. That was one of the reasons. But if you ask me, I'll say this quite openly, he realised at the time how important these people were and how crucial they were to his ability to obtain his own political goals and in terms of helping Croatia's defence as a whole. I'm sorry if I'm trailing off here into some sort of interpretation rather than telling you what you expected me to say, but I do believe that this is something that casts a truly different light on the transcript itself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You provide very long answers. They should be shorter. I use the opportunity from my colleague's question, and this will not be taken out of your time, Mr. Karnavas, rest assured. I use this opportunity to raise an issue that seems to me extremely relevant, and your very words raised -- focused my attention on this issue. I see that there was this meeting between Tudjman and the delegation of Herceg-Bosna, and under item 1 it is stated that: "The Community of Herceg-Bosna is going to give its full support to the recognition and the final establishment of the Republic of Croatia." That's item 1. But based on this, since you were very close to President Tudjman, you held very high functions indeed, I'd like to know the following: Why did the Republic of Croatia fail to recognise officially at one point in time the Republic of Herceg-Bosna? And I'm raising this issue based on the recent model where you had various countries that recognised Kosovo. Why is it that back then Croatia did not want to or was not able to officially recognise the Republic of Herceg-Bosna? Could you answer this question?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, if you meant the Republic of Herceg-Bosna, and sometimes this term was used to imply the organisation of Croats, as far as I know Croatia never seriously thought about recognising this as an independent republic. As far as Bosnia and Herzegovina is concerned, the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina as a sovereign state, Croatia was the first state, if I'm not mistaken, that recognised Bosnia and Herzegovina at the moment when Bosnia and Herzegovina sought the recognition. I'm again speaking off the cuff. At that moment Bosnia and Herzegovina had not yet sought recognition either from Croatia or the international community.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So you are telling us that at no point in time did Croatia envision to recognise the Republic of Herceg-Bosna, that it was never a concern of the then leaders of Croatia and that you never heard this possibility being mentioned.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I heard a reference being made to a possibility of the break-up of Bosnia and Herzegovina and separation of different parts of Bosnia according to different models. I heard that at various international negotiations because reference was made to that, but the unilateral recognition by Croatia of the organisation of Croats in the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina that appeared under different names, one of them being Herceg-Bosna, I never attended any such meeting that a reference was made to that, and I don't know that such a possibility was ever seriously considered by the Croatian leadership.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Mr. Zuzul, I would like -- following up on the question that my colleague Prandler has asked, I would like to take you back to this Presidential transcript and to page 34 at the top. I think it would simply not be fair if I did not give you the opportunity expressly to comment on this. Here, Mr. Tudjman is quoted in the first paragraph as saying this: "It seems to me, therefore, that just as we have taken advantage of this historic moment to establish an independent internationally recognised Croatia, I believe that it is time that we take the opportunity to gather the Croatian people inside the widest possible borders." I wonder how this is to be understood in your view.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Judge Trechsel, before he answers the question, because you skipped a page, I think, and I was going to ask because it should follow -- it should have followed Judge Prandler's quotation to read also page 33 because I think you cannot fully answer Judge Prandler's question without reading the top paragraph of 40 -- of 33. And then with that, then we can go on to 34 because it's sequential. So if that's okay, otherwise I'll go back. But I think without page 33, I'm afraid we're cherry-picking at this point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: If you want to read it, read it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well, here's the part. It says: "And create," this is picking up where Judge Prandler left off, the continuity of the thought. It is: "And to create a statement, therefore, out of the remaining part around Sarajevo where mostly Muslims and some Catholic Croats would stay which would resemble a small historical land of Bosnia. It would therefore be a buffer zone in the demarcation of Serbia in Croatia, and in such conditions, it would have to rely on Croatia to a large extent. That would also satisfy international actors who are now surely seriously counting, as you mentioned, on Serb policing for that Muslim element, Islamic element, in Yugoslavia whose intention is to establish with the help of Tehran and Tripoli an Islamic state in Europe." That's the part that I wanted in, in keeping that we talked earlier about what he had mentioned about the policing of Muslims, the US -- the Americans' position. And so with that in mind, I think that's -- that puts context into what -- because it seems to me there is some connection to all of this. But I don't want to lead the witness.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The way I experienced this transcript and the overall discussion that transpires from it was that Tudjman primarily responded to the proposals that were presented to him in a very concrete form immediately prior to that. In the 19 items he speaks about various variants. One of them is the cantonisation; the other is republics. All sorts of things are mentioned because at that moment all the options are on the table. As far as the international community was concerned, there was also an option to divide Bosnia-Herzegovina because the documents that we saw before had already been known. In that context, Tudjman presents his discussion and from time to time he presents his own personal views according to which the Western world does not want an independent Muslim state or that, in one way or another, the Western world wanted to have a buffer zone. I would call this considerations rather than proposals. As for the paragraph that the Honourable Judge pointed to, one can see here that he makes a clear distinction between the internationally recognised Croatia, which means that he speaks with a certain degree, if you allow me my own interpretation, a degree of pride because he knew that very soon after that Croatia would be recognised. He speaks in one way about the international borders, and he speaks in another way which doesn't lend itself to an easy interpretation about the Croatian territory or the Croatian interest, territory, or the territory where Croats lived, and he primarily implies 30 -- or the 28 municipalities. It seems to me that one can see the difference very clearly, especially within the context of the previous question. He does consider certain possibilities and options, but he leaves room for future decisions and reactions. And there are also areas where he's very firm and categorical, one of them being the borders of Croatia. I think that Tudjman could not be as categorical and as proud at the moment about the recognition, the upcoming recognition of Croatia, if he had thought at the time that the international borders of Croatia would change. Tudjman was not naive. That's at least what we thought of him. And if he had thought in that way he would have appeared naive. On the one hand he speaks about the recognised borders and the recognition of Croatia, and on the other hand he speaks about different ways to solve the situation in Bosnia and Herzegovina and the different options for that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please proceed, Mr. Karnavas.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Any other questions? Otherwise, we'll go on to the next document. And I think from now on where we -- where there's a need I think it's perfectly acceptable, and in fact the best thing is for the Trial Chamber to ask their questions as we go through this.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: The next one is P 00130. This is another so-called presidential transcript. And just to save a little time we can see this is 3 March 1992, and we can see from the very first page that your name is on -- is on as one of the -- somebody that was present at the meeting. P 00130. Do you have it?

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR ZUZUL [Resumed]
utterances.text: [In English] Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, because I don't want to lose too much time on this one, have you had an opportunity to read this -- this particular transcript?

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR ZUZUL [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And the one part that I want to focus on just very briefly before I ask you for any other things that you may wish to point out, on page 65, at the second paragraph, it says: "I think that this is a big problem that should be resolved urgently, namely the problem of communication. The Croatian War Navy, the Sixth Operational Zone, and especially in the context of the problem of Herzegovina." Now, this is several months after the previous transcript that we saw. Can you tell us how the situation had changed if at all in Croatia vis-a-vis the JNA and the aggression that we spoke about yesterday?

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR ZUZUL [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that moment the overall situation had changed to a certain extent. Croatia was a recognised state and UNPROFOR zones had already been established in certain parts of Croatia or their establishment was under way, so there was no military danger in Croatia. The situation was frozen, in military terms, at that point. However, there was still a direct threat in the area around Dubrovnik. Even after the recognition of Croatia, the UNPROFOR mandate never extended to the area around Dubrovnik and south of Dubrovnik. We're talking about, me and others, which was the main purpose of this meeting, was in relation to the general problems of the army. I and the others who were with me had all just come back from a visit to the territory around Dubrovnik, and we spoke about the problems faced by the defence there, one of the problems being communication between the different branches the Croatian army, more concretely between the navy and land army, and the impossibility of formal communication with the units. I better say -- I don't know whether I can call them units in formal terms, but with the volunteers in Herceg-Bosna from the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina, those that I referred to a while ago. And this is what this particular sentence refers to as well as the rest of my presentation. I would like to add to that the group that I was with was dealing with the psychological and information activities; i.e., problems in communication with the different parts of the military were an integral part of our everyday work.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: You're going to have to slow down a little bit now. Now we might be going a little bit too fast, but is there anything else on this transcript? Otherwise we'll move on to the next document. I only mention that because you were present.

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR ZUZUL [Resumed]
utterances.text: As for the context in which this happened, I believe that a lot has already been said about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, if we go to the next document, 1 -- it's P 00131, and the Prosecution says that this particular document is relevant because this transcript records discussions by the senior Croatian military command and shows Croatian logistical assistance of both arms and military units to the Bosnian Croats. And there's a reference to page 27, and we can see that on that particular page there are references to sector Dubrovnik. Now, before we get into the specifics of this, if we just look at the very first page we'll see that you were present at this meeting. This is the following day from the previous transcript, 4 March 1992, and all sorts of other individuals are present, as well, including an individual by the name of Daidza, and perhaps you could begin by telling us did you know this person, who was and what position he held? Just very briefly.

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR ZUZUL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I met Mr. Daidza during one of my visits to the southern front. I don't know whether this was immediately prior to this event. At the moment when I met him, he was the commander of a unit which mostly consisted of Muslim volunteers. At the moment when we met them, they were in training in Croatia. If I'm not mistaken, this was somewhere near Makarska. Maybe in Backa Polje, but I'm not a hundred percent sure. But I know for a fact that he was the commander of that unit of Muslim volunteers who fought together with the Croatian volunteers against the J -- the Yugoslav Army.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. I'm going to have to ask you to slow down a little bit, but you say Muslim volunteers. Would they be Muslim volunteers from Bosnia-Herzegovina, or are they Muslim volunteers from Croatia?

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR ZUZUL [Resumed]
utterances.text: From Bosnia and Herzegovina. From Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, you also mentioned the word "training." I take it that you meant military training.

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR ZUZUL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I believe that this was primarily military training.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. And just prior to that you had pointed to what has been previously marked as 3D 03171. That's the map itself. And you had pointed towards the area of Dubrovnik. At this -- so I want to focus your attention, and perhaps you might be able to comment. On page 25 of this transcript where you say -- when Daidza says: "I was assigned a task to arrange the valley of the Neretva River together with the other commanders because it was our very last defence line. I would like to give a brief statement." And then he gives a statement, and then on page 27, at the very last sentence there is a reference from a Luka --

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR ZUZUL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Djanko.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: -- Djanko, thank you, where he talks about the zone of responsibility of Dubrovnik sector covers only the short preliminary territory of the municipalities of Dubrovnik, Metkovic, Ploce -- I always have problems with this one.

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR ZUZUL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Vrgorac.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Vrgorac in Western Herzegovina. And then it goes on: "It is specific about of few elements, Neum and Herzegovina cut it off and it is shallow for the Defence. The Dubrovnik municipality is encircled and facing subjective problems in commanding, and I will say a few words. "There are actions in Herzegovina without written orders issued by the staff, and I'm already there with two of my brigades. Croatian people of Herzegovina are incapable to defend the line from Mostar to Popovo Polje, and I think that they have approximately 22.000 barrels of artillery which is enough. I'm going to say a few words," and then there's a further discussion. Now just so I'm clear, do these reflect what you were saying yesterday with respect to Neum and the difficulties of covering the entire Croatian -- southern Croatian territory?

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR ZUZUL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This is a very specific illustration of my own words. I can provide you an example and give you an episode. The first time I met Mr. Djanko down there he was the commander of the Croatian army in the area but not of the navy. According to some information, Yugoslav tanks were moving towards Opuzen -- or, rather, towards the line on the Neretva River. At the moment when we arrived, he was considering the possibility of blowing up a bridge on the river Bistrina in the area. However, when we looked at a map we could see that this would not make any strategic sense, because if he blew up that bridge, he would have prevented their passage through the narrow territory of Croatia. But they could proceed and went on moving to the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina. What I'm trying say is this: It was absolutely clear that it was absolutely impossible to defend that territory unless the defence of the part of the territory in Herzegovina was involved in that overall defence, because it was from that particular area that all the attacks came from.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Okay. Thank you. We're going to move on to the next three documents. I will try to cover them in succession, so I'll just point out some relevant passages and then ask you to comment on them if that's okay with the Trial Chamber just to save some time, because they relate more or less to the same matter. So we'll be looking first at P 00205. This is from the Security Council. It's 15 May 1992. Before we go to the document, is Croatia at this point in time sending troops into Bosnia and Herzegovina to attack the Sarajevo government?

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR ZUZUL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course not.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Have they sent in troops at this point in time to attack the Muslim people?

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR ZUZUL [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. And you just told us just previously that in fact there were Muslim volunteers who were being trained in Croatia, assisting Croatia in its defence against the JNA which was launching attacks from the territories of Bosnia and Herzegovina onto Croatia; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR ZUZUL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Right. Now, if we look at this Security Council Resolution, and if we go to the second page under item number 2, it says: "Welcomes the effort -- the efforts undertaken by the European Community in the framework -- framework of the discussions on constitutional arrangements for Bosnia and Herzegovina under the auspices of the conference of Yugoslavia; urges that the discussion be resumed without delay; and urges the three communities in Bosnia and Herzegovina to participate actively and constructively in these discussions." And it goes on and on? First question is: Were you aware of -- of these activities? There was -- there were undergoing discussions concerning the constitutional arrangements in Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR ZUZUL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. And at any point in time -- this is a foundational question for future questions. At any point in time, were you involved in any sorts of activities, negotiations, discussions, drafting of -- of agreements or what have you, that were based in part -- were due to the -- the discussions on the constitutional arrangements of Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR ZUZUL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Most certainly over the entire period of time, on several occasions. At this point in time, I was in a certain way involved in negotiations and talks.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now let's look at point number 3. It demands that all forms of interference from outside Bosnia and Herzegovina, including the units of the Yugoslav People's Army, JNA, as well as elements of the Croatian army cease immediately and that Bosnia and Herzegovina neighbours take swift action to end such an interference and respect the territorial integrity of Bosnia-Herzegovina." First question, to your knowledge were there elements of the Croatian army on the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina and, if so, where would they have been located at that point in time in light of the circumstances and the activities that you've already discussed thus far?

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR ZUZUL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't have any concrete information about that, but I believe that there were elements of the Croatian army on the territories of Bosnia and Herzegovina. I don't have any reason to doubt this report, but it is also absolutely clear from the overall situation that at that moment they were fighting exclusively against the JNA, which was at the time in the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina, which is also confirmed by this particular Resolution.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, we're going to get other Resolutions, but if you could just help us out a little bit because yesterday we talked about the UN and their lack of effort to send combat troops to defend the territorial integrity and the lives of Croatians as a result of the aggressive actions taken by the JNA. Assuming, assuming, and you told us that you were in that area and you know it very well, so we have the foundation for that. You were in the military, so we have the foundation for that, as well, so let's assume that those elements of the Croatian army had withdrawn from that area around Dubrovnik and further up by Neum and what have you, and let's assume for the sake of our hypothetical, but we will see later on that in fact that was the case, that the JNA did not withdraw from that territory, what would have happened to the southern part of Croatia?

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR ZUZUL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yesterday I said that at that time there already was enough compelling information to the effect that it was the plan of the Serbian army, because the Yugoslav army at that time was completely controlled by the Serbian leadership, to establish the border along the Neretva River. It is my impression that had it not been for the volunteers from Herzegovina, Croats, and the volunteers of Muslim ethnicity who fought side by side with them, again I have to say this is my personal impression, and the assistance they received from the Croatian army, and the elements of the Croatian army, that they would not have been able to achieve this goal militarily. Now, as for the fate of Bosnia and Herzegovina, as for the course that the peace talks would take, this is something that we can only guess and speculate, but it is a fact that all the peace talks about Bosnia and Herzegovina had as their starting point the fact that the Serb side was in control of certain territory, and at times they side-stepped the issue as to how Serbs actually got to hold this territory.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Let me just move on for the sake of -- there's a point number 4. We've seen this before where it talks about -- it says: "Demands that those units of the Yugoslavia People's army and elements of the Croatian army now in Bosnia and Herzegovina must either be withdrawn or be subject to the authority of the government of Bosnia-Herzegovina or be disbanded and disarmed with their weapons placed under effective international monitoring, and request the Secretary-General to consider without delay to what international assistance could be provided in this connection. First, let me ask you this starting with the latter part of this segment. What if any assistance, what international assistance, was provided at this point in time in that particular area?

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR ZUZUL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Primarily monitoring it seems to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Were the monitors in a position to fight back the JNA should they continue with their attacks on Croatia?

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR ZUZUL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that they did not have this kind of mandate at that time. I'm sure that they didn't have it at that time. They didn't have the forces to do it either. And we know, I think from the judgements rendered by this Tribunal, that even when they had the forces they were not in a position to intervene and to prevent some major humanitarian catastrophes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, the next two documents are dated --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] A follow-up question if I may on the document we've just been reviewing. It is document 205 if I'm not mistaken. Is this the right document, Mr. Karnavas?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Correct, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the Resolution, on page 2 in the English version, item 4, it is demanded that the Croatian army units in Bosnia be withdrawn. It is something we've discussed for hours, for dozens, maybe hundreds of hours. To your knowledge, sir, were there units of the Croatian army in Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that at that time there were elements of the Croatian army in some areas of Bosnia and Herzegovina. Now, as to how one can define those elements, it's a different issue, but they all fought side by side with all those who were trying to defend themselves against the Yugoslav army and the Serbian aggression as I have already said. We in the Republic of Croatia, for instance, welcomed this resolution. At that time, I was in the Foreign Ministry. Why did we welcome it? Because this resolution offers two options. One, for the Yugoslav army to withdraw from Bosnia and Herzegovina. At that time, there was still some optimism among the international institutions, and some hoped that this could actually come to pass. In that case, the question of any elements of Croatian army remaining there would become immaterial. They would have nothing to do. But if that did not happen, the Resolution goes on in paragraph 4 as it continues offering another option for those forces to be placed under the authority of the government of Bosnia and Herzegovina. Your Honour, I can vouch that at that time we were already in contact with Bosnia and Herzegovina with the aim of operationalising the conclusions stemming from this Resolution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was only referring to the month of May 1992. For the rest, we'll see later. Thank you very much. Mr. Karnavas, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, the next two documents are May 1992, and again, they sort of touch upon the same issues that we've discussed, and if we look on page -- page 2 of P 00232, sort of in the middle of the page it says: "Deeply concern also at the developments in Croatia, including persistent cease-fire violations and the continued expulsion of non-Serb civilians and at the obstruction of and lack of cooperation with UNPROFOR in other parts of Croatia." If you could assist us a little bit. What are they talking about when they say the continued expulsion of non-Serb civilians? Are we talking about in Croatia? What part? What are they talking about?

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR ZUZUL [Resumed]
utterances.text: They're talking about the events in so-called UNPROFOR zones. Those were parts of Croatia that had been occupied by Serbs where the so-called Republic of Serbian Krajina had been set up. The international forces arrived in the areas, yet despite that, the expulsion of non-Serbs continued in that zone and in other zones, and when they're talking about the lack of cooperation, it is obvious that at that time what happened was that the self-proclaimed authorities in those occupied forces were refusing to cooperate with UNPROFOR.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well, were those self-proclaimed authorities being assisted by any particular armed force, or were they just capable on their own to conduct those expulsions?

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR ZUZUL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right from the beginning, they received direct support and assistance from the Yugoslav People's Army. They received weapons from them. The command structure was for the most part taken over from the Yugoslav army. One of the commanders in the area in -- in the Knin area was Ratko Mladic before he moved to Bosnia and Herzegovina, so it is no secret that it was a mix of self-proclaimed leaders who advocated the idea of Greater Serbia and the Yugoslav army, which in the meantime had dropped every pretense of the effort to save Yugoslavia. They merely occupied Croatia, and soon they moved to occupy Bosnia and Herzegovina too.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And again before I -- before I ask my next question concerning this particular document, can you tell us at this point in time how much of the -- of Croatian territory is occupied? It might be relevant because sometimes in this courtroom we tend to forget the percentage of the country and the devastation that Croatia underwent.

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR ZUZUL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't want to pretend to be an expert. From what I've read and from the documents that I received in my diplomatic career, the international documents, the percentage of the territory was between 25 at the lower end, but the figure that was quoted most often was 30 per cent of the Croatian territory. That would be one-third of the overall territory of Croatia that was occupied at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. And we see now in this -- in paragraph 2 -- I mean on page 3, item 2, I'm sorry, page 3 item 2 it says: "Demands that any elements of the Croatian army still present in Bosnia-Herzegovina act in accordance with paragraph 4 of Resolution 752 very quickly." Had the situation say, just in the southern part of Croatia, where we talked about earlier, had that changed in the 15 days between the document that we saw earlier, that is P 0025 and this one P 00232, had the situation changed on the ground at all?

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR ZUZUL [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. The situation did not change, but in the meantime the diplomatic activities between Croatia and Bosnia and Herzegovina were stepped up, and they would soon result in the signing of the agreement that would fully meet the demands of the UN Security Council.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I'm told that there's a wrong number in the transcript. It should be P 00205.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is P 00232.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Yes. For the record, for the transcript, I probably misspoke and that's why it was written down. I was referring to earlier.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Now when we get to this document P 00233, which is the last document in this series, it's dated the same date, and you told us that the JNA has not left at least the areas in Bosnia and Herzegovina where they're attacking Croatia. Now, if we look at -- I just wanted to point a couple of things out again. So we can take a reality check over here, or do a reality check. In paragraph 10: "As regards the withdrawal of elements of Croatian army now in Bosnia and Herzegovina, information currently available in New York suggests that no such withdrawal has occurred. UNPROFOR has received reliable reports of Croatian army personnel in uniforms operating within and as part of military formations in Bosnia-Herzegovina. The Croatian authorities have consistently taken the position that the Croatian soldiers in Bosnia-Herzegovina have left the Croatian army and are not subject to its authority. International observers do not, however, doubt that the position of Bosnia-Herzegovina are under the control of the Croatian military --"

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR ZUZUL [Resumed]
utterances.text: [In English] To the portion.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: To the portion -- I'm sorry, the portion I can't read. "The portion of Bosnia and Herzegovina under the control of the Croatian military and it's whether -- whether belonging to the local territorial defence, to paramilitary groups, or to the Croatian army. It is unclear in the circumstances how their withdrawal or disbandment as required by the council can be achieved." We spoke of Mr. Daidza. Was Daidza under the -- to your knowledge, that is - if you can answer the question; if not, we won't bother - but was he under the control of the Croatian military or the Croatian authorities or the Croatian army?

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR ZUZUL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I couldn't give you an answer to that question. I think it was quite clear to me who Daidza and his volunteers were fighting, but as to under whose control he was, I couldn't really venture an opinion.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR ZUZUL [Resumed]
utterances.text: But Mr. Daidza was from Bosnia and Herzegovina. That is a notorious fact. Everybody knew that, myself included. He was from some place in Central Bosnia, if I'm not mistaken.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] A general question, Witness. At the time you no doubt read the Resolutions of the Security Council, I suppose. Your department within the ministry kept close scrutiny of anything that was written at the time.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Surely. At that time, I was at the Foreign Ministry at the time. We were familiar with those Resolutions, and we were trying to take steps in accordance with those Resolutions. Now I'm talking about the Foreign Ministry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As you know, those Resolutions result from different information coming from the international forces present on the ground, from other sources, and so on and so forth. In your position, in your capacity, did you observe at any time major mistakes in the Resolutions when certain facts were mentioned? Do you have specific cases in mind where you could say that what was written down was obviously wrong, inaccurate, based on unreliable information? Do you have in mind one or two examples that you could give us from the top of your head?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, Mr. President, I can't now think of any Resolutions or reports of the UN Secretary-General such as this one where I spotted some major errors. If there were any such cases, we reacted while the Resolutions were in the process of being drafted. At times, it appeared that the idea behind the Resolutions was to establish some kind of a balanced approach towards -- where all sides would be treated in the same way, and to us who knew what the situation was like on the ground, they did not seem an accurate reflection of that. I can tell you that because I had direct relations, good relations, with a number of international representatives. I would sometimes bring that up. At times, I would officially put -- make an official protest, but most often I would receive the following reply: They were there to establish facts and not to judge what is going on, who is to blame and who is not. It seemed to us that this approach was not always productive, but that may have been just our impression because, after all, I was there to represent the Republic of Croatia, and I allow the possibility that I was subjective in my approach. But I couldn't really say that I noticed any major glaring errors in those documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Before the break --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: If I could, just one last point on this document, and we'll take our break.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Sticking with the same document, because this is 233, because you mentioned Mladic, and I think it might be relevant here. If we look at paragraph number 5 on page 2, it says: "The bulk of JNA personnel who were deployed in Bosnia and Herzegovina were citizens of that republic and were not, therefore, covered by the Belgrade authorities' decision of 4 May to withdraw JNA from Bosnia-Herzegovina. Most of them appeared to have joined the army of the so-called Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Others have joined the Territorial Defence of Bosnia and Herzegovina" -- I can't read that next word -- "which is under -- which is under the political control of the Presidency of that republic. Others may have joined various irregular forces operating there." Now, you said earlier -- you talked earlier about General Mladic, who was in Croatia at one point, JNA officer. Now, can you explain a little bit about what is being said in paragraph 5, why it might be significant about the JNA personnel?

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR ZUZUL [Resumed]
utterances.text: In an effort to report objectively, I was talking about it a moment ago, it is my interpretation that the Secretary-General in this report as it is worded, that the members of the Yugoslav army from Bosnia and Herzegovina have now joined the newly formed armies. In actual fact, nothing changed. Those were the same troops. They retained their equipment; I think the equipment is actually mentioned somewhere in this report by the UN Secretary-General, and they had the same command structure. And unfortunately time would tell. I think this is the first time that General Mladic is actually referred to in a document originating from the United Nations, but as time went by we went on to see under whose command he operated and what he actually did. So this was just pretense. The same troops remained there under the same command.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you. That's it, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. We'll take a 20-minute break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Karnavas, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PRANDLER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Mr. Karnavas, to stop you, but before we break I didn't want to take your time. I only would like to have a question from Mr. Zuzul, and it is about a clarification. During the very last minutes of -- of the witness, you spoke and he spoke about some of the Resolutions of the United Nations Security Council, and I believe it was page 74, lines 1 and 2, that -- that Mr. Zuzul you mentioned that, and I quote: "I was there to represent Croatia," et cetera. And now my question of clarification is the following: According to -- to your -- I mean the summary of what we have received, there is not very much clearly stated, if you will, also posted in New York or only in Geneva. This morning you -- I mean, previously you mentioned that you were posted in Geneva as the permanent representative of Croatia to Geneva. Now, I gathered from your last statement that -- that if you were also in New York as representing Croatia as a permanent representative or only as a member of delegation, et cetera. So my question is to clarify if you were permanently in Geneva or sometimes you participated at the General Assembly sessions in New York or at the meetings of the Security Council. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. When the Resolutions were passed, I was with the foreign ministry. I was, in actual fact, assistant minister. I had started dealing with the negotiations already. I had not yet been appointed ambassador. Soon after this, I became deputy foreign minister. You talked about the position of ambassador to the UN in Geneva. I was appointed on the 1st of February, 1993, to that particular position. However, even while working as assistant and deputy foreign minister in Geneva, I was a regular member of our delegations in New York, as well, and I was quite involved in the work of our delegations, and I took part in discussing all the Resolutions on the Croatian side, needless to say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PRANDLER
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you, Judge Prandler.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And I wanted to point out something on page 74, line 24, because it was translated as -- in an effort for those folks to be objective, and I believe my colleague tells me that you used the word "Pokusaj," if I'm pronouncing that correctly. Could you please tell us whether that means "effort" or "attempt," because it may be a slight variation. It may be slightly nuance, but just to have a more accurate -- what did you exactly mean when you were asked the question about the reports? Were they making an effort, or were they attempting? I don't want to put words in your mouth, but I'm told that you actually used the word. We don't have a Croatian transcript. So if you could think back?

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR ZUZUL [Resumed]
utterances.text: [In English] I would say that they were making efforts.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. All right. Now, if we could go to the next document, and we're probably going to move through the next couple of documents rather quickly so we can get some more substantive areas. The next one is a P document for Prosecution, P 00263. This is a presidential transcript. Now, this is dated 15 June 1992, and of course the Prosecution in its exhibit list indicated that the relevant pages for them are 66 to 67 and that this transcript shows army of Republic of Croatia units being sent into Bosnia and setting up check-points there. Now, if I could direct you to that page, page 67, it also shows, by the way, that you were present. I don't know if you recall being present, but in any event, the first page shows that you were present. Page 67, as I understand it, you had an opportunity to read not just the English version but also to make some comparisons with the Croatian version, and it might be of some significance, I don't know, we'll leave it up to the Trial Chamber, but could you look at that, the very last paragraph where it starts: "The numbers of theft and larceny cases has also increased." Did you notice anything missing, any words missing in that?

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR ZUZUL [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's true, I was at this meeting. Naturally having read the transcripts it came back to me. It has been 16 years since, after all. However, when I read both English and the Croatian versions, I noticed that the English is missing a word which in this case might change the overall meaning. In the English it's page 67. In the Croatian -- I don't know exactly how the pages were marked, but I think it's 714. Anyway, the word "return" is missing. Therefore, if we try to translate this paragraph over here there is a word missing, the word "return," which can be translated into English -- well, I am certainly no expert, but to the extent that I can tell, it could be translated in two ways perhaps, "withdrawal," which is I think the word that most people would have used in this case, or "return," which is another possibility. If you add that word to the paragraph, no matter if you actually opt for the word "withdrawal" or the word "return," I think this changes the meaning entirely, and the paragraph shows that those elements of the Croatian army that were in Bosnia and Herzegovina were now returning home and while withdrawing were perpetrating certain crimes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. And with respect to the -- to the issue of check-points -- well, perhaps you could read the paragraph itself, which is only a few lines.

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR ZUZUL [Resumed]
utterances.text: [In English] Excuse me, the same paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Yeah. And you can read it in Croatian. It can be translated or you can read it in English, however you feel more comfortable. Croatian is the original language of the transcript, so ...

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR ZUZUL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Maybe I'll read it in Croatian so maybe we'll get new translation then.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR ZUZUL [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Interpretation] "Cases of theft and larceny have been on the increase. The movable property, too, has been stolen, and in the last cases at local check-points machines and equipment has been moved over from Herceg-Bosna where units and individuals who were involved over there along various front lines while returning to Croatia have been hauling in as war booty tractors, and all other kinds of agricultural machinery, et cetera. "However," and that's the next paragraph, "However, we have set up very effective check-points here, and I can now say that we have been particularly effective at putting a stop to this kind of practice."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. All right. Can you, being there, and now that we have the context and having read it and spotted the error, can you tell us when they say "we have set up check-points here," what are they talking about? What kind of check-points, and what does "here" mean in this context?

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR ZUZUL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't tell you exactly where the check-points were. I simply don't know. However, looking at the overall context, I think these are check-points in Croatia itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. All right. Let's go on --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Just for the record, Mr. Karnavas, wouldn't it be good to mention that it is Mate Lausic who is speaking here? It's not Boban. It's not the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Right. Right. I should apologise. I should have done that. I'm just getting a little tired but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Of course. We all are.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: -- you're absolutely correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. And now just for the record, who is that individual so we know?

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR ZUZUL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think at this time he was the commander of the military police of the Croatian army.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. All right. Now, if we go on to the next -- next document, P 00336. This is a presidential transcript dated 21 July 19 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: We have to change the folders.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: 21 July 1992, and first context. At this point in history, what is happening in Croatia? Has the JNA withdrawn? Have the attacks stopped, or is it -- and has the territory up to 30 per cent, as you've indicated, does Croatia have total control over its territory within its internationally recognised borders?

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR ZUZUL [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were no considerable changes in Croatia at this time. Large tracts of Croatian territory were still under occupation. There was nothing much going on in terms of warfare, as far as I know, since all of those were by now UNPROFOR-controlled areas. However, there wasn't anything in particular moving in a good, positive direction either. Nevertheless, relations were changing between Croatia and Bosnia and Herzegovina. Bosnia and Herzegovina had by this time been internationally recognised. It had been recognised by Croatia as well. In the context of this story, one thing that strikes me as worth mentioning is that at a referendum before Bosnia and Herzegovina was established, there were only Bosniaks and Croats participating. The Serbs refused to be involved. President Tudjman issued a public call on Croats in Bosnia and Herzegovina to go to that referendum and to vote in favour of an independent Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina. Soon after the proclamation, Croatia recognised Bosnia and Herzegovina. We started with diplomatic consultations immediately. This document is in relation to the first major meeting following the recognition. However, in the context of the Resolutions that I have been talking about, there is one thing that I would like to note. Sometime in mid-June President Tudjman and President Izetbegovic issued a joint statement. I was with President Tudjman when we prepared the statement. Among other things, the statement also dealt with issues mentioned in the Secretary-General's letter as well as in the Resolutions of the Security Council. Croatia wanted to act on those documents immediately. So this gives you the general background. There was a lot of diplomatic activity going on. This meeting was agreed and eventually held between the leaders of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina and the leaders of the Republic of Croatia in Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Now -- thank you. Let me walk you step by step, but I'm happy that you put that into context because let me use this to segue into my next question. The Prosecution in the 62 ter description in describing this particular presidential transcript, and I'll use a word that they attribute to me that is "spin", this is what the Prosecution says: That this transcript --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour, as I objected earlier this afternoon, I'm also going to object again to this now.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: There's no point in putting these preparatory comments and criticisms. He can ask the question. If he can point him to the page and say -- if -- assuming it's otherwise a fair question, there's no reason for these other preparatory remarks.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I am entitled -- I am entitled -- this is the Defence, Mr. President. I am defending allegations. The allegation -- the spin by the Prosecutor who wasn't there at the time is suggesting that -- that Tudjman is -- presses the Bosnian president. The gentleman is particularly familiar. That's their spin. He's going to comment.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: This is further coaching of the witness, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: How is it coaching of the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Because I'm now telling you what the Prosecution position is, so you can be sure to disagree with that. That's your queue to disagree.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: This is objectionable.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Just ask the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Your Honours, let's take a reality check. I met with the witness. I went through the documents. If I wanted to coach him, I would have coached him back then.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Maybe you did.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: This is absolutely ridiculous, and this Prosecutor has met with every single witness, gone through the documents, and we've seen them testify. So I'm -- they allege a joint criminal enterprise. They allege that Tudjman is pressing the Bosnian president, entering into a particular agreement, which is the very next document. That's their spin. I'm entitled to -- I'm entitled to point that out because the gentleman can comment. To suggest that I'm suggesting is utterly and patently ridiculous, and I'm being generous at this point.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, I do suggest it, and also, Your Honour, I ask the Chamber and not just Judge Antonetti. I ask all the Chamber in fairness. Remember back during the Prosecution case and when the Prosecution put on its witnesses. I didn't say, and I'm telling you, Mr. Witness, what the Prosecution case is, and this is the answer I want you to give, and if you look at paragraph so-and-so of our indictment, this is the Prosecution's theory. I didn't preface my questions, and the Prosecution counsel didn't in that way. You ask a witness to come in. You put questions to the witness. You don't argue your case. You don't say, I'm telling -- I'm putting your spin on it. You ask questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: It's called burden of proof, Your Honour, burden of proof. They are alleging. They have the power. They draft that indictment the way they want it. They decided to put the spin on this particular presidential transcript in order to get it in. That's their interpretation. I'm not inventing anything. That's their invention. They got to proof that. I'm attacking. I'm defending. That's -- so if he thinks that's the case --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Karnavas, the Judges are thinking about how to speed up trials, and the both of you have just illustrated the need for Judges to intervene at times. Mr. Karnavas, you want to highlight one point. Very well. In order to do so, you tell the witness, "Look at this transcript. There is this particular sentence." He can say yes. He can say no. He can say, "I don't know." Thereafter, afterwards you say, "well, it appears in the indictment that this is being alleged," and then we can move forward.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Very well, Mr. President, but it's not in the indictment. It's in their description of the evidence, but very well. And I understand that the description is not evidence, and you'll see a motion that I filed where I objected to these characterisations. That's parted of this -- my whole attack on the Prosecution case, that in trying to get in evidence they've had to put certain descriptions as to what they believe the evidence shows. So that's part and parcel. And then when I objected to that, they came back and they said, "No. Our -- our characterisations are part of the evidence." But I take your point. Let me move on. Let's go straight to the document. Okay. Let's everyone calm down a little bit.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: 21st of July, 1992, there's a discussion, and I just want to focus you very briefly because we're going to go on to the next document. On page 59, we have Dr. Franjo Tudjman, who is the president, and there he's -- he says, and I quote: "Mr. President Izetbegovic, our time is limited, so can we finish with this part of the discussion as the base -- as the presumption for further interstate conversations, that both delegations agree that the status of the Croatian people in Bosnia-Herzegovina should be organised on the basis of three constitutive units of Bosnia and Herzegovina; and second, that the defence forces of the Croatian Defence Council are considered to be an integral part of the defence forces of Bosnia and Herzegovina and that they are to be represented in the command, the Joint Command of Bosnia-Herzegovina." Now, can you tell us given the position that you held and your involvement, can you tell us exactly why is President Izetbegovic pursuing this sort of policy, if you will, with President Izetbegovic at the time -- I mean, President Tudjman, why is he pursuing this with President Izetbegovic?

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR ZUZUL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I attended this meeting. I think it was a very important meeting. I think it clearly illustrates the principles that President Tudjman applied when he was thinking about Bosnia and Herzegovina as well as when acting in relation to Bosnia and Herzegovina. He accepts President Izetbegovic as the president of a sovereign neighbouring country recognised by Croatia. He is here expressing his concern about the position of the Croats there, the Croats as a constituent nation in Bosnia and Herzegovina. He's here tabling a proposal that was anyway based on the proposal put forward by the international community, and I'm referring to Cutileiro's plan to the effect that the Croats within Bosnia and Herzegovina should be on an equal footing with all the other ethnic groups there. He also goes on to propose that the Croatian armed forces in Bosnia and Herzegovina should be placed under a Joint Command to be exercised by the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina so that they might be better able to defend themselves from aggression. I think this very paragraph does a great job illustrating President Tudjman's position at the time. Not just at the time. This moment is when it was actually formulated, but what I've been trying to say yesterday and today is this: My impression from the very beginning of the crisis in Bosnia and Herzegovina and onward was that Mr. Tudjman's policies were defined by these three principles, and all three can easily and to great advantage be seen in these sentences contained in the proposal.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. And just before we get down to the next document, did President Tudjman --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for counsel, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Did President Tudjman intend to subordinate, to subordinate, the Croatians and the Croatian army in Bosnia and Herzegovina, the HVO, under whatever army existed for the Sarajevo government, or when he says "integral part," did he have some other intention?

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR ZUZUL [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. He wanted both for the Croats to enjoy an appropriate position in Bosnia and Herzegovina's government and its institutions including the BH army command and for the Croatian defence forces to become and integral and indivisible part of the BH army forces [as interpreted]. I think it is impossible to view these two issues separately. He wanted them to effectively become one and the same army, but he also wanted to have a Croat involved in the command structure.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. I'm told that it was the defence forces, not the BH army forces. Is that what you meant? Because my disadvantage is I don't understand Croatian, and my colleague here is pointing out at page 85, line 18. So if you could look at that and please tell us again, because we're talking -- there are some nuances here, and I just want to make sure because I can see the Prosecution busily writing away for the cross-examination. I certainly don't want to give him any ammunition as a result of something lost in translation.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreters note, it was interpreted as defence forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Let's go to the next document. We're told -- we'll move on. It's okay now. We'll move on. P 0 --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could I ask a question, Mr. President? As I'm unable to monitor both my words and the interpretation at the same time, and I have noticed some errors, and given the fact that between my testimony today, my testimony tomorrow, and my next testimony months will have gone by, I have to apologise for my ignorance, but may I please be granted a chance to inspect a transcript of my evidence and all the other documents, especially in view of the fact that I'm perfectly aware that I'm not allowed to contact the Defence, the OTP, or the Tribunal? Is this something that is doable, and is my request a logical one? I do apologise, but this just brought the issue to mind.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Transcripts are public and they normally can be accessed by everyone. So by the time you return in July, you will have ample time through the internet to access the transcripts of today's hearing. No problem at all. Unless the system breaks down. You never know.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: If we could get to the next document, P 00339, because this is connected to our previous document. P 00339. It's dated July 21, 1992, and we could see that there's a title to it. "Agreement on friendship and cooperation between the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina and the Republic of Croatia." Now again just to make sure that we're clear, that everybody is crystal clear, by this point Croatia has recognised Bosnia's independence; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR ZUZUL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Within those internationally recognised borders?

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR ZUZUL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, we don't have that much time to dwell on this, nor do we need to, but if we could go to paragraph number 8. Paragraph number 8. And I will go through it step by step. "In consideration of the continuing aggression of the Serbian and Montenegrin military forces against the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, but also largely against the republic of Croatia from the contiguous areas of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, the President of the Presidency of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina and the President of the Republic of Croatia call upon the international community, and in particular the United Nations, the European Community, and the United States of America, to take real and efficient steps to vigorously stop the aggression against their States, to prevent further loss of human life, persecution and expulsion of their citizens and the destruction of property." Let's pause right here. By this point when this was drafted, when they say "in consideration of the continuing aggression," was the aggression continuing in a manner in which it's stated in this paragraph?

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR ZUZUL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Definitely.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. And I know that we talked about this a little bit. They're asking the United Nations, European Union, and the United States of America to take real and efficient steps to vigorously stop the aggression. I mentioned this before. Let me ask it again. By -- by the date of this agreement, July 21, or thereafter did the United States send in combat troops to protect the territorial integrity of Croatia and/or Bosnia and Herzegovina against the JNA or whoever was the aggressor at the time?

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR ZUZUL [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. At that point in time, nobody ever considered the sending of troops that would fight the Yugoslav People's Army, and if I may comment upon this paragraph, because I directly participated in the drafting of all this, this is a direct annotation on behalf of both presidents to the United States of America because President Clinton had become president, and even before that President Tudjman had sent him a letter expressing his belief that without direct involvement on the part of the United States of America, the crisis would not be solved, and that is why we put this in the agreement between the two presidents. Both agreed with that. And if I may add a comment to that with regard to this document for which I believe that it is extremely important. Not that there was no pressure from one side to another, but, rather, we negotiated about -- about all this, and I don't really know what we're to use. We measured our words carefully the whole day, not just paragraphs but words, especially Mr. Trnka on the Bosniak side and I and the others on the Croatian side, and this is really a good example of our joint work. The presidents signed the document that had been prepared by the respective delegations that comprised representatives of both states. In other words, this document was prepared in a very, very serious manner.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. With that in mind, let's go on to the next part of paragraph 8. "With this objective in mind, both States will sustain their -- will sustain their past successful cooperation and continuous coordination of the defensive activities in" -- I underscore "in" -- "the contiguous zones of the two States." Question number one is this an accurate statement? That is, was there past successful cooperation between these two folks with respect to activities in the contiguous zones?

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR ZUZUL [Resumed]
utterances.text: The successful cooperation implied any attempt to prevent the Yugoslav People's Army from achieving their overall strategic goals, and I mean by that preventing them from establishing new borders or taking up the area all the way down to the Neretva River.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Let's go on. "Aware of the fact that both States are threatened, unless aggression against them is urgently stopped by further destruction and annihilation of their state entity and integrity, the two states will, should the efforts of the international community remain ineffective, take all necessary steps in order to establish broader cooperation in the military sphere and coordinate military operations in order to definitely --" I think this might be "repel the danger threatening them." So was this an accurate --

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR ZUZUL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, with respect to broader cooperation in military -- in the military sphere and coordinate military operations, since you were part of the negotiating process, can you tell us at least at that stage what was envisaged? I know we have the presidential transcripts, and we can probably glean from that conversation, but you being a participant, can you help us out here?

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR ZUZUL [Resumed]
utterances.text: What this meant at the moment was every possible form of cooperation between the Croatian army and the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina. And I'm not referring to the Croats in Bosnia and Herzegovina but the Croatian army. There were even talks, and the paragraph leaves the possibility open, although not explicitly, about joint military actions whenever those were needed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. And then just finally on paragraph 9 very quickly, it says that there was an agreement to have a protocol on the establishment of diplomatic relations between the two states at embassy level signed immediately. Did that occur?

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR ZUZUL [Resumed]
utterances.text: [In English] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, let's move on to the next document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is an interesting document for me, a document that was discussed with other witnesses before, and of course I am going to seize the opportunity to ask this question to somebody who took part in the generation of the document. The previous document on the presidential transcript, and let me note that the meeting lasted 10 hours and 15 minutes, we have proof that the document was produced right after the meeting and that the witness participated in the production of the document. Here is my question: This document is signed by both presidents. It is an agreement of friendship and cooperation between the two republics. For your country, was this document distributed? Was it published in the Official Gazette of your republic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
