utterances.text: [Interpretation] The document was made public on the same day, or maybe the following day. I'm not sure -- sure, and I'm not an expert either to tell you whether this type of agreement should have been published in the Official Gazette, whether it falls under that category.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine. I had another question. This is an international agreement. According to your law, unfortunately I didn't have the time to check it myself, but was this document due to be ratified by the parliament, or was it up to the president to commit his country to an international agreement without necessity to -- for the document to be ratified?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe that for this document no ratification was necessary. In my view, under the then-prevailing constitution the president of the republic could have signed this agreement without this document being ratified by the parliament. I believe that under the current constitution of the Republic of Croatia, this type of agreement could have -- could be signed even by the Minister of Foreign Affairs, which for that matter is the case in other states as well. But I believe that given his constitutional competencies, the president could sign such a document today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Several revolutions of the Security Council are referred to in this document, particularly the one on the 13th of July, 1992. Did you officially send this document to New York for information so that the international community be informed? And in the next document - Mr. Karnavas was maybe about to talk about this document - another Resolution is mentioned. So did you send that document to the international community so that everybody could be made aware that from now on the HVO army was opposed to the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina as provided for in paragraph number 6 of the document?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We informed the international community about this document on the following day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] These were all my questions. Mr. Karnavas.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Now if we could turn to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Hold on a second. Mr. Praljak is on his feet. I don't know why.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, then, very well. If --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well, let me just go on.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: The next document is 1D 02295. Okay. Okay. I will --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Praljak.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, your words have been translated into Croatian as the document saying that the HVO would be opposed to the BiH army. That's how it has been translated into Croatian. Can this please be taken into account?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's not what I said. There has been an error in the interpretation. What I said is that the HVO army, according to the document, was an integral part of the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina. That's what I said. So I'm calling upon the interpreters to be very vigilant because on several occasions we've seen the importance or the significance of -- of nuances such as a comma or full stop. So, please, if you note any problems or misinterpretation, please don't hesitate to let us know for -- in everybody's interests.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: May I point out that exactly the same error appears in the English transcript, so what Your Honour has just said will constitute a correction of that as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well indeed, because when I speak I don't necessarily check the transcript in English. I look at you rather than -- than at the screen. I'd rather look at the Defence counsel than at my screen. Mr. Karnavas, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] Thank you. First, I have to thank General Praljak for that correction, and that's an important one, and we thank him very much. And we thank that he insisted on making that correction. The dangers of circumstantial evidence sometimes, of jumping to conclusions.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: 1D 02295. That's the next document. It's dated 6 August 1992, obviously some time after the agreement we've seen, and it says here at the very top: "I have come to the territory of the Republic of Croatia at the decision of the Presidency of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina." And if we look at the bottom, we're talking about Fikret Abdic. Do you know who this person is?

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR ZUZUL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I knew Mr. Abdic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. And we'll hear more about him through other witnesses. Now, if you go further down, I don't want to -- he does indicate: "My task is to organise activities which are at this moment of particular importance for Bosnia and Herzegovina." Skipping the next sentence and going down it says: "In view of the recently signed interstate agreement, we consider Croatia to be the right place to set up a number of activities which are of consequence for both republics. With your consent, we intend to establish a Main Staff for providing support to Bosnia and Herzegovina with its headquarters in Rijeka and several regions -- regional staffs in different locations in Croatia." And then if we go to the very last paragraph, first sentence: "We kindly ask that you adopt a decision legalising the work of our Main Staff and regional staff in the Republic of Croatia, the locations of which will be determined by mutual agreement." My first question is when he's talking about the recently interstate agreement, were there any other agreements other than the one that we just saw that presumably, if we are to believe some, Alija Izetbegovic was pressed to sign? Were there any other agreements, or is this the agreement that Mr. Abdic is referring to?

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR ZUZUL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that Mr. Abdic was referring to the agreement that we had just looked at and discussed, because this letter is only a logical part of the implementation of this agreement. He may even be referring to one of the earlier agreements, the one that was signed in June that I have mentioned, but I would rather be inclined to say that it -- it is referring to the last agreement we discussed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. And when he's talking about setting up a Main Staff, with the intent to establish a Main Staff, what did you -- if you can tell us, what do you think he means by that? What is he asking? Are we talking about the military or civilian sector? What are we talking about?

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR ZUZUL [Resumed]
utterances.text: My interpretation would be that this primarily applies to the military and logistical centre. As you can see in the map, Bosnia-Herzegovina has a border only with Serbia from which aggression came from, and the eastern part of Bosnia and Herzegovina for that matter was occupied by the Serbs. So the only the connection of Bosnia and Herzegovina with the rest the world goes through the Republic of Croatia, and that's why all the numerous refugees and all the supplies went through the Republic of Croatia, and I'm talking about the humanitarian aid, medical aid, food, and clothes. All those things went through the Republic of Croatia. Unfortunately, the Republic of Croatia and Bosnia and Herzegovina were exposed to an unjust decision on the part of the international community. And I would like to apologise to the Honourable Judge and correct myself. A decision or an embargo on the import of arms had been imposed on the Republic of Croatia and Bosnia and Herzegovina. Both the republics were not -- were poorly armed, and they were facing a very well-armed enemy, which was the Yugoslav People's Army. Bearing that in mine, everybody has to be clear and understand that they resorted to various means to arm themselves. I wouldn't be able to testify about the ways and means, the arms reached the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina because I'm not well-informed about that. But whoever who looks at the map will understand how it went. A lot has been written about that. My understanding is that a large part of the international community was actually aware of the fact that they had issued a very unjust decision, and by issuing that decision they had prevented the state from arming itself and defending itself. A large part of the international community turned a blind eye, I would say, when it came to the supply and transport of both weapons as well as all the other different military equipment through the territory of Republic of Croatia into the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina. If you will allow me another comment, I would like to say that the Republic of Croatia really had wanted to annex part of the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina, then it would not have made much sense to issue a decision to the effect of helping it to arm itself, and I'm sure that it did help in every possible way.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. And tomorrow we'll see some documents to that effect. All right. Now, if we could go through the next document, P 0386, P 00386. We see that this is 13 July. This is a week after Mr. Abdic made that request. This is Resolution 771, and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar, how much time, please, has been used by Mr. Karnavas?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. If you look at this document and you look at the next document, which is P 387, and we look at the other one -- the other document that follows that, the other P document, P 00406, if we can just spend a few seconds looking at them. They're all from the UN. The first one, 386, is 13th of August, the second one is 13th of August, and the third one is 25th of August. If I can just ask you very briefly, had the situation changed on the ground, that is, had the -- had the JNA or the -- or elements of it, had it left the -- the territories of Bosnia and Herzegovina, and had the danger ceased to exist, concerning Croatia, that is?

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR ZUZUL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Nothing major changed in Croatia, and as for Bosnia and Herzegovina, it became more and more evident that the Yugoslav People's Army gradually occupied territories and violated all international rules. In one of the items of this Resolution, makes an explicit reference to ethnic cleansing. Where is that? I think it's item 2, which mentions the operations of the Serbian army in the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina at that moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: You're referring to which document, but there are three documents.

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR ZUZUL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Document 386.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. All right. But say, for instance, in the other document where they're talking about, for instance, 406, you'll see under page 3, paragraph number 3: "Demands further that those units of the Yugoslav People's Army and elements of the Croatian army now in Bosnia and Herzegovina must either be withdrawn or be subject to the authority of the government of Bosnia and Herzegovina." Okay. Now if we pause a little bit at this, it seems to me from your previous answer that the Yugoslav People's Army is still there. Would it be fair to say the elements of the Croatian army remained -- seemed to be in -- within Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR ZUZUL [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I may explain. This is a -- a Resolution of the General Assembly, which differs from the Resolution of the Security Council. It differs because it doesn't have an executive force and also by the way it was passed. It took a longer time to prepare this Resolution, and it always does then for the Resolutions of the Security Council. If that wasn't the case, then it would be a totally superfluous to mention the Croatian forces because the agreement that deals with this issue evokes the already-signed Resolutions, which means that the conditions of the Resolutions had been met. I can tell you that I'm aware of this Resolution. When the diplomacy of Bosnia and Herzegovina launched an initiative to issue this Resolution Croatia provided its full support to this initiative. I personally took the text of the proposal of the Resolution to President Tudjman, and he authorise I had me to instruct our diplomats to give their full support to the representatives of Bosnia and Herzegovina when this Resolution was being passed. As you know, it takes 100 -- over 180 States or over half a majority of the Assembly of the United Nations pass a Resolution. This Resolution was more political than executive in nature, but as far as the diplomacies of the Republic of Croatia and Bosnia and Herzegovina were concerned, this meant that this was an implementation of our friendship agreement, and we in Croatia fully supported the passing of this Resolution.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Well, I see our time is up for the day, Mr. President. I don't want to keep anyone here any longer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Karnavas, you've used three minutes -- three hours, sorry, and 45 minutes. So you'll have one hour and 15 minutes left tomorrow. Now, what about tomorrow? I'm turning to the other Defence counsel. Will you cross-examine this witness? If you wish to cross-examine this witness, you'll have two hours and 30 minutes. Mrs. Alaburic, is --

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. I believe that it would be very good to use Mr. Zuzul's time, because Mr. Zuzul knows a lot about topics that are very relevant for us. I do intend to put several questions to Mr. Zuzul. I have half an hour at my disposal, and I've asked the Defence teams of Mr. Pusic and Mr. Stojic to give me their time if I find this to be necessary and of benefit to the Trial Chamber, and I'm also going to talk to the other Defence teams if they're not interested in cross-examining to give me their times.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. So you will cross-examine this witness during an hour and a half. Mrs. Nozica.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. For the time being I do not intend to -- to examine the witness. In any case, we will decide by tomorrow, and if we do not intend to examine we will give our time to Mrs. Alaburic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, we expect not to have any questions. Perhaps Mr. Praljak will have one or two very short, but it is still under consideration. More probably not than yes, but if, we are talking really about couple of minutes.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, as things stand now, we are not going to have any questions. We will make our final decision tomorrow. And as Mrs. Nozica has already told you, in that case we will give our time to Mrs. Alaburic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Anyway, tomorrow we will conclude at 6.30 at the latest. Judges may need some time to ask questions as well. If there isn't enough time left, you know that the hearing will resume on the 18th of July. Witness, the 18th of July is a Friday. The Prosecutor will have five hours to cross-examine you. Of course there have been administrative issues, objections, and so on, and it appears that we won't have enough time to finish everything on Friday. We may have to continue on Monday morning. Therefore, you will have to stay over during the weekend between the 18th of July and the 20th. I hope this is not going to cause any difficulty for you since, in particular, weekends in The Hague are pretty pleasant when the weather's nice. So please make the necessary arrangements to be at the disposal of the Chamber on Friday, the 18th of July, and most probably on the following Monday because after the Prosecutor's cross-examination, there will most probably be redirect. So we need to schedule for two days and not just one, just for your prior information. I know July is still far away, but I just wanted to give you that information so that you can make arrangements. Now, you may have planned some holidays in July. I don't know. It may not be very convenient for you, but it is impossible to do otherwise. The Prosecutor was not in a position to start his cross-examination this week. This is obvious. This is all I wanted to say at this stage. We will resume the hearing tomorrow at 2.15 in the afternoon. Let me reiterate the recommendations I gave you yesterday. No communication with anyone while you're still under oath. Thank you. See you tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Thursday, the 8th day of May, 2008, at 2.15 p.m.
